1552	# Money Map — raffle.fun (`Raffle` ERC-1167 clone + `RaffleFactory`)
1553	
1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).
1563	
1564	## 1. Assets
1565	| Asset | In | Out |
1566	| --- | --- | --- |
1567	| USDC `quoteToken` (trusted canonical; blacklistable/pausable) | `buyEntries` L224 `safeTransferFrom(msg.sender)`, gross = `entryCount * 1e6` | `redeemWinningTicket` L342 (CashWon → ticket owner), `refundTickets` L369 (→ caller = owner), `releaseSponsorProceeds` L380 (→ `sponsorRecipient`), `releaseProtocolFees` L390 (→ `protocolTreasury`). All via `_transferQuote` (destination-screened) |
1568	| Prize ERC-721 (untrusted contract) | `RaffleFactory::createRaffle` L128 `prize.safeTransferFrom(sponsor, clone)` → `Raffle::onERC721Received` (status → Active) | `redeemWinningTicket` L334 (NftWon → ticket owner; `transferFrom` + `ownerOf` check), `releaseSponsorPrize` L404 (CashWon/Refunding → `sponsorRecipient`; `transferFrom` + `ownerOf` check). NOT destination-screened at release time |

1652	# The 0xSimao Method
1653	
1654	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1655	
1656	## The core thesis
1657	
1658	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1659	
1660	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1661	
1662	| Drift | Shape |
1663	| --- | --- |
1664	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1665	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1666	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1667	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1668	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1669	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1670	
1671	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1672	
1673	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1674	
1675	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1676	
1677	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1678	
1679	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1680	
1681	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1682	
1683	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1684	
1685	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1686	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1687	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1688	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1689	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1690	
1691	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1692	
1693	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1694	
1695	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1696	
1697	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1698	
1699	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1700	| --- | --- | --- |
1701	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1702	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1703	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1704	
1705	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1706	
1707	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1708	
1709	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1710	
1711	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1712	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1713	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1714	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1715	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1716	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1717	
1718	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1719	
1720	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1721	
1722	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1723	
1724	Canonical sequences to run:
1725	
1726	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1727	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1728	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1729	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1730	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1731	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1732	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1733	
1734	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1735	
1736	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1737	
1738	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1739	
1740	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1741	
1742	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1743	
1744	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1745	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1746	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1747	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1748	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1749	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1750	
1751	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1752	
1753	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1754	
1755	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1756	
1757	After every finding:
1758	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1759	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1760	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1761	
1762	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1763	
1764	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1765	
1766	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1767	
1768	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1769	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1770	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1771	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1772	
1773	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1774	
1775	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1776	
1777	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1778	
1779	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1780	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1781	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1782	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1783	
1784	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1785	
1786	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1787	
1788	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1789	
1790	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1791	
1792	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1793	
1794	## Do not report
1795	
1796	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1797	# Lens 1 — Accounting Desync
1798	
1799	You own the single largest class of 0xSimao's High findings: **a tracked total that no longer equals the thing it claims to track.**
1800	
1801	Other lenses own math, ordering, and access. You own the gap between what the protocol *records* and what it *holds*.
1802	
1803	## The shape
1804	
1805	Value moves. A variable is supposed to move with it. It does not — or it moves in one branch and not the other, or it is written before the math that depends on its old value, or it is reinitialized when it should have accumulated.
1806	
1807	Everyone downstream then computes against a lie. Early actors withdraw more than they are owed. The protocol becomes short. The last user out cannot be paid.
1808	
1809	## Attack surfaces
1810	
1811	**Hunt the missing decrement.** For every transfer out, find the variable that should have decreased. If none exists, or if the decrement lives in only one of several exit paths, you have it. Check `withdraw`, `redeem`, `emergencyWithdraw`, `claim`, expiry paths, liquidation paths, and cross-chain variants — the forgotten one is rarely the main path.
1812	> *Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry*
1813	> *Missing Update to `omnichain.totalAvailableLiquidationAmount` in `withdrawUser`*
1814	> *Method refundPlayers doesn't update `_lockedETH` in WinnableTicketManager*
1815	
1816	**Hunt the one-sided branch.** Any `if`/`else` where one branch writes an accounting variable and the other does not. Any early `return` that skips a write. Any `try`/`catch` where the failure path leaves state half-updated.
1817	> *Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`*
1818	
1819	**Hunt write-before-read.** A variable mutated before the calculation that needed its pre-state. Burning shares before computing share value inflates the price for the burner. Transferring before setting a rate distributes at the wrong rate.
1820	> *`burnSharesToWithdrawEarnings` burns before math, causing the share value to increase*
1821	> *`Voter::finalize()` incorrect rewards distribution due to transferring WETH before calling `distributor::setTokensPerInterval()`*
1822	
1823	**Hunt the untracked balance.** A token or ETH balance that is real but has no variable representing it, or is represented by `balanceOf(address(this))`. Live balance reads are donatable and shared across users.
1824	> *Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency*
1825	> *Lost withdrawals due to `ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance*
1826	> *Incorrect withdraw queue balance in TVL calculation*
1827	
1828	**Hunt the reinitialization.** State that should accumulate but gets overwritten when a user re-enters. Run deposit → withdraw → deposit on every position-holding structure and check whether the second deposit resets something the first established.
1829	> *Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`, getting profit stuck for cds depositors*
1830	> *Cancelling rounds after finalizing will lead to incorrect `globalTokenAllocPerIDORound` tracking*
1831	
1832	**Hunt the mismatched pair.** Two amounts that must be equal but are computed differently — burn `newAmount` but redeem `amount`, debit from `msg.sender` but read state from `user`, credit shares from one formula and debit from another.
1833	> *`BasicVault::_redeem()` burns newAmount but redeems amount, allowing attackers to drain the vault*
1834	> *`Borrowing::redeemYields` debits `ABOND` from `msg.sender` but redeems to `user` using `ABOND.State` data from `user`*
1835	> *Mismatch between yield amount deposited in shares calculation and `getAccountYieldBalance()`*
1836	
1837	**Hunt the unreturned value.** A function returns the actual amount moved and the caller ignores it, assuming the requested amount. Fee-on-transfer, partial fills, capped withdrawals, and AMM slippage all make requested ≠ actual.
1838	> *Providing liquidity to the AMM does not check the return value of actually provided tokens leading to locked funds*
1839	> *Fee on transfer tokens transfer less tokens than what is stored in the receipt on deposits*
1840	> *`FlashSwapRouter::emptyReserve()` and `emptyReservePartial()` functions return incorrect values*
1841	
1842	**Hunt value with no owner.** Fees, dust, residuals, and yields that accrue to no one and can be claimed by anyone — or by nobody, permanently.
1843	> *Protocol fee from Market.sol is locked*
1844	> *Yield from LRTs are forever stuck in the protocol and cannot be withdrawn*
1845	> *In the `unlockProtectedListing()` function, the interest that was supposed to be distributed to LP holders was instead burned*
1846	> *Interest generated by last bond will not go to anyone when liquidating as there is no bond amount to collect it*
1847	
1848	## Required closing test
1849	
1850	For every lifecycle in the money map, run `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]`: every user withdraws in the worst possible order. If the protocol is short by any amount, trace back to the step that leaked and report *that*, not the failed withdrawal.
1851	
1852	## Every finding needs the balance sheet
1853	
1854	State the shortfall concretely: after N steps, users can claim X, the contract holds Y, X > Y by Z. No numbers = LEAD.
1855	# Shared Lens Rules
1856	
1857	## Bundle contents
1858	
1859	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1860	
1861	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1862	
1863	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1864	
1865	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1866	
1867	## Mandatory reasoning protocol
1868	
1869	Four markers. Each has a trigger. When the trigger fires you MUST emit the marker before continuing. Markers live in your working text — they do NOT go inside FINDING/LEAD blocks.
1870	
1871	| Trigger | Marker | Content |
1872	| --- | --- | --- |
1873	| You open a function that moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Explain in plain English what a user gives, what they get, and which totals change. No Solidity jargon — no `safeTransfer`, `mload`, `shares`, `wad`. Where you have to reach for a Solidity term to stay accurate, mark that spot: that is where the bug is. |
1874	| You stop on a line whose purpose is not immediately obvious | `[Why: <file:line>]` | One question that drills past "because that is how it is written." If your answer restates the code, ask again. Stop when the answer exposes the implicit belief the code rests on. |
1875	| A path reads as clean, or a guard looks sufficient | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Three concrete attacker moves against it. Specific addresses, values, and states — never abstractions. |
1876	| You finish a lifecycle from the money map | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | Walk every user withdrawing in the worst order. State explicitly whether the last one gets paid in full, and if not, by how much the protocol is short. |
1877	
1878	Heavy use of these is what produces the audit. Skipping them yields surface-level scanning, which is the failure mode of every junior auditor. The orchestrator checks marker counts.
1879	
1880	## Saturation is mandatory
1881	
1882	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1883	
1884	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1885	
1886	## Do not report
1887	
1888	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.

1890	## Output
1891	
1892	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1893	
1894	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.

1899	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1900	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1901	path:
1902	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1903	  2. state changes to Y
1904	  3. actor does Z
1905	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1906	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1907	```

1909	```

1911	smell: what you found
1912	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1913	description: one sentence on the trail
1914	```

1917	
1918	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.

1552	# Money Map — raffle.fun (`Raffle` ERC-1167 clone + `RaffleFactory`)
1553	
1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).

1606	## 4. Invariants
1607	- I1 `quoteToken.balanceOf(clone) >= accountedQuoteBalance()` at all times (solvency; DESIGN "remainder must be allocated without loss").
1608	- I2 Pre-terminal (Active / Drawing / NftWon / CashWon before settlement): `unsettledPot == totalEntries * ENTRY_PRICE`.
1609	- I3 Refunding: `remainingRefundLiability == Σ_{unburned tickets} (lastEntry - firstEntry + 1) * ENTRY_PRICE`; the last refunder is paid in full and the bucket reaches exactly 0.
1610	- I4 Settlement: `cash + sponsor + fee == grossPot`; fee = floor(5%); cash = floor(80%) in CashWon, 0 in NftWon; sponsor = remainder.
1611	- I5 The prize NFT leaves exactly once, to exactly one party: NftWon → winning-ticket owner; CashWon/Refunding → `sponsorRecipient`.
1612	- I6 Refund branch and win branch are mutually exclusive per clone.
1613	- I7 Ticket ranges partition `[1, totalEntries]`; exactly one ticket contains `winningEntry ∈ [1, totalEntries]`.
1614	- I8 Status is monotone: AwaitingPrize → Active → (Drawing → (NftWon | CashWon | Refunding)) | Refunding. No back-edges, no second request, no re-roll.
1615	- I9 Time windows (DESIGN): buy `< endTime`; request `[endTime, endTime + 2d)`; callback `< drawRequestedAt + 2d`; refunds open exactly at the applicable deadline; empty raffle: sponsor any time, anyone `>= endTime`.
1616	- I10 Only VRF determines the winner: no actor can choose, preview-and-react, censor-and-retry, or bias the drawn entry.

1618	- I12 Assets never move between raffle clones; the factory never holds assets.
1619	- I13 Redemption: only the current ticket owner; burn is atomic with delivery; any delivery failure reverts everything.

Factory views `raffleImplementation()` / `isRaffle()` are called from every `_update` and `_transferQuote`.
1650	- Constants: ENTRY_PRICE 1e6; fee 500 bps; cash 8000 bps; refund batch ≤ 100 tickets; sale ≤ 30 d; request window 2 d; callback window 2 d; callback gas 300k; 30 confirmations.
1651	- Dependency sources present under `packages/contracts/node_modules/` (OZ 5.6.1, Chainlink 1.5.0 `VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase`, `IVRFV2PlusWrapper`). The wrapper implementation itself is not vendored — reason from the trusted canonical VRF v2.5 wrapper.
1652	# The 0xSimao Method
1653	
1654	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1655	
1656	## The core thesis
1657	
1658	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1659	
1660	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1661	
1662	| Drift | Shape |
1663	| --- | --- |
1664	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1665	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1666	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1667	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1668	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1669	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1670	
1671	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1672	
1673	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1674	
1675	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1676	
1677	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1678	
1679	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1680	
1681	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1682	
1683	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1684	
1685	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1686	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1687	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1688	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1689	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1690	
1691	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1692	
1693	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1694	
1695	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1696	
1697	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1698	
1699	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1700	| --- | --- | --- |
1701	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1702	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1703	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1704	
1705	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1706	
1707	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1708	
1709	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1710	
1711	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1712	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1713	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1714	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1715	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1716	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1717	
1718	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1719	
1720	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1721	
1722	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1723	
1724	Canonical sequences to run:
1725	
1726	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1727	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1728	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1729	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1730	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1731	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1732	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1733	
1734	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1735	
1736	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1737	
1738	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1739	
1740	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1741	
1742	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1743	
1744	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1745	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1746	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1747	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1748	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1749	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1750	
1751	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1752	
1753	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1754	
1755	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1756	
1757	After every finding:
1758	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1759	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1760	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1761	
1762	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1763	
1764	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1765	
1766	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1767	
1768	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1769	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1770	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1771	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1772	
1773	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1774	
1775	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1776	
1777	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1778	
1779	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1780	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1781	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1782	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1783	
1784	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1785	
1786	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1787	
1788	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1789	
1790	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1791	
1792	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1793	
1794	## Do not report
1795	
1796	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1797	# Lens 2 — Shares, Exchange Rates & Redemption
1798	
1799	You own the conversion between **claims** (shares, receipt tokens, positions, notes) and **value** (assets). Every deposit mints a claim; every withdrawal burns one. If the two directions disagree by even a little, someone extracts the difference repeatedly.
1800	
1801	## The shape
1802	
1803	The exchange rate is a ratio of two things the protocol tracks. Break either side — inflate the numerator, deflate the denominator, or change one without the other — and mint/redeem become a money pump.
1804	
1805	## Attack surfaces
1806	
1807	**Round-trip every path.** Deposit X, immediately withdraw. Do you get more than X? Do it again in a loop. Any path where a round trip is profitable at zero risk is a drain, and looping makes it critical.
1808	> *DarkPoolAssetManager can be drained by looping over join(), joinSplit() or swap() with only some initial amount*
1809	> *`_rebalanceWithdraw()` mechanism in glAVAX allows arbitrage opportunities by changing the shares/AVAX ratio*
1810	> *REBALANCER_ROLE can drain funds by rebalancing in a loop in the BorrowingVault*
1811	
1812	**Attack the denominator.** The share price divides by a total. Ask what happens when that total is zero, one wei, or donatable. Live balance reads in the denominator are donation attacks.
1813	> *SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate*
1814	> *`OffchainExchange::swapAmm()` does not validate that `txn.priceX18 > 0`, allowing donation attacks*
1815	> *`state.cumulativeDepositsMultiplierX18` may become 0 or negative, leading to loss of funds*
1816	
1817	**Check burn order against value computation.** Shares burned before the value calculation change the very rate used to pay out. Establish whether the payout uses pre-burn or post-burn supply, and whether that is what the protocol intends.
1818	> *`burnSharesToWithdrawEarnings` burns before math, causing the share value to increase*
1819	> *Incorrect redeemAmount Is Accounted Due To Not Accounting For The Exchange Rate*
1820	
1821	**Verify the ERC4626 contract, if the protocol claims it.** `maxDeposit`/`maxMint`/`maxWithdraw`/`maxRedeem` must reflect real limits including pauses, caps, and mint limits. `preview*` must match the actual result. `withdraw`/`redeem` with no slippage parameter is a real finding when the rate is manipulable between submission and execution.
1822	> *`maxDeposit` doesn't comply with ERC-4626*
1823	> *`VaultV2::withdraw/redeem()` are vulnerable to slippage, so another function could be added to protect users*
1824	> *`ManagedLeveragedVault.sol::deposit()` is missing slippage control*
1825	> *`LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart_test::addPrincipalToCommitmentGroup/burnSharesToWithdrawEarnings()` are vulnerable to slippage attacks*
1826	
1827	**Break the receipt.** Receipt tokens, position NFTs, and notes carry claims. Ask whether transferring one moves the associated rewards/debt correctly, whether it can be redeemed twice, and whether the claim can be separated from the obligation.
1828	> *Reward Token Loss for LPs During NFT Position Transfer*
1829	> *Staked tokens inside FluidLocker can be withdrawn without calling Unstake*
1830	> *`Fluid (SUP)` can be withdrawn from the Locker while the unlock flag is false*
1831	> *Reusing the same rho and pubKey in different deposits leads to lost tokens*
1832	
1833	**Redeem into the wrong state.** Redemption at expiry, after a slash, while paused, mid-epoch, or after another user's redemption has already changed the pool. His richest vein: the redemption function that is correct in the normal case and wrong in exactly one terminal state.
1834	> *Admin new issuance or user calling `Vault::redeemExpiredLv()` after `Psm::redeemWithCt()` will lead to stuck funds when trying to withdraw*
1835	> *Withdrawing all `lv` before expiry will lead to lost funds in the Vault*
1836	> *Withdrawing after a slash event before the vault has ended will decrease `fixedSidestETHOnStartCapacity` by less than it should, so following users will withdraw more than their initial deposit*
1837	
1838	**Follow the token to the wrong recipient.** Redeem to `user` while burning from `msg.sender`, send collateral to the caller instead of the position owner, route fees to a stale address.
1839	> *liquidateDefaultedLoanWithIncentive sends the collateral to the wrong account*
1840	> *Attackers can claim deposits to vaults if users specify the router as receiver and don't withdraw shares after*
1841	
1842	## Every finding needs the arithmetic
1843	
1844	Show the rate before and after with concrete numbers, and the extracted amount per round trip. "The rate can be manipulated" is a LEAD; "1e18 donated moves the rate from 1.00 to 1.05, extracting 4.7e18 over three loops" is a finding.
1845	# Shared Lens Rules
1846	
1847	## Bundle contents
1848	
1849	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1850	
1851	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1852	
1853	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1854	
1855	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1856	
1857	## Mandatory reasoning protocol
1858	
1859	Four markers. Each has a trigger. When the trigger fires you MUST emit the marker before continuing. Markers live in your working text — they do NOT go inside FINDING/LEAD blocks.
1860	
1861	| Trigger | Marker | Content |
1862	| --- | --- | --- |
1863	| You open a function that moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Explain in plain English what a user gives, what they get, and which totals change. No Solidity jargon — no `safeTransfer`, `mload`, `shares`, `wad`. Where you have to reach for a Solidity term to stay accurate, mark that spot: that is where the bug is. |
1864	| You stop on a line whose purpose is not immediately obvious | `[Why: <file:line>]` | One question that drills past "because that is how it is written." If your answer restates the code, ask again. Stop when the answer exposes the implicit belief the code rests on. |
1865	| A path reads as clean, or a guard looks sufficient | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Three concrete attacker moves against it. Specific addresses, values, and states — never abstractions. |
1866	| You finish a lifecycle from the money map | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | Walk every user withdrawing in the worst order. State explicitly whether the last one gets paid in full, and if not, by how much the protocol is short. |
1867	
1868	Heavy use of these is what produces the audit. Skipping them yields surface-level scanning, which is the failure mode of every junior auditor. The orchestrator checks marker counts.
1869	
1870	## Saturation is mandatory
1871	
1872	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1873	
1874	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1875	
1876	## Do not report
1877	
1878	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1879	
1880	## Output
1881	
1882	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1883	
1884	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1885	
1886	```
1887	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1888	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1889	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1890	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1891	path:
1892	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1893	  2. state changes to Y
1894	  3. actor does Z
1895	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1896	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1897	```
1898	
1899	```
1900	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1901	smell: what you found
1902	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1903	description: one sentence on the trail
1904	```
1905	
1906	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1907	
1908	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.
1909

1553	
1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).

1652	# The 0xSimao Method
1653	
1654	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1655	
1656	## The core thesis
1657	
1658	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1659	
1660	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1661	
1662	| Drift | Shape |
1663	| --- | --- |
1664	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1665	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1666	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1667	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1668	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1669	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1670	
1671	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1672	
1673	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1674	
1675	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1676	
1677	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1678	
1679	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1680	
1681	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1682	
1683	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1684	
1685	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1686	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1687	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1688	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1689	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1690	
1691	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1692	
1693	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1694	
1695	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1696	
1697	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1698	
1699	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1700	| --- | --- | --- |
1701	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1702	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1703	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1704	
1705	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1706	
1707	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1708	
1709	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1710	
1711	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1712	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1713	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1714	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1715	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1716	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1717	
1718	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1719	
1720	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1721	
1722	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1723	
1724	Canonical sequences to run:
1725	
1726	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1727	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1728	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1729	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1730	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1731	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1732	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1733	
1734	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1735	
1736	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1737	
1738	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1739	
1740	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1741	
1742	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1743	
1744	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1745	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1746	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1747	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1748	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1749	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1750	
1751	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1752	
1753	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1754	
1755	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1756	
1757	After every finding:
1758	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1759	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1760	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1761	
1762	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1763	
1764	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1765	
1766	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1767	
1768	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1769	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1770	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1771	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1772	
1773	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1774	
1775	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1776	
1777	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1778	
1779	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1780	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1781	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1782	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1783	
1784	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1785	
1786	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1787	
1788	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1789	
1790	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1791	
1792	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1793	
1794	## Do not report
1795	
1796	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1797	# Lens 3 — Temporal Cohorts & Distribution Fairness
1798	
1799	You own the question that produces 0xSimao's most distinctive findings: **when value is distributed pro-rata among a changing set of holders, who actually gets it?**
1800	
1801	Other lenses ask whether the total is right. You ask whether the *split* is right, and whether someone can arrive just in time to take a share of value they did not earn — or leave just in time to dump a loss on whoever stays.
1802	
1803	## The shape
1804	
1805	Accumulated value is distributed using a *current* snapshot: current total supply, current deposits, current balance. But the value accumulated over a *past* period during which the holder set was different. Anyone who joins between accrual and distribution is paid for time they were not present.
1806	
1807	The mirror image is equally productive: a loss realized against current holders lets the actor who caused it exit first.
1808	
1809	## Attack surfaces
1810	
1811	**Join immediately before a distribution.** For every reward, yield, fee, liquidation profit, or expansion event: can an actor deposit in the same block (or one block before) and claim a pro-rata share of value accrued earlier? Flash loans make the capital requirement irrelevant, so size is never a defense.
1812	> *Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking*
1813	> *Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders*
1814	> *`increaseNetworkTotal()` allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction*
1815	> *Cds depositors profit up to the strike price is not redeemable as the total cds deposited amount is not increased*
1816	
1817	**Leave immediately before a loss.** Can an actor whose position created a shortfall exit before it is realized, leaving remaining holders to absorb it?
1818	> *Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers*
1819	> *Total cds deposited amount is incorrectly modified when cds depositor is at a loss, leading to stuck USDa*
1820	
1821	**Audit every cumulative index and rate.** Index-based accounting is correct only if the index advances exactly once per unit of time/value and every user's snapshot is taken at the right moment. Check: can the index be advanced for free? Is `lastUpdate` written every time the index is? Is the user's checkpoint set on deposit, on transfer, and on receiver-different-from-sender deposits?
1822	> *Malicious user can call `borrowing::calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated*
1823	> *Unconditional lastUpdated advance in RangePool.sync leads to loss of streamed BMX when pool liquidity == 0*
1824	> *Accumulated profit/losses by the cumulative value is not dealt with in `borrowingLiquidation::liquidationType1()`, leading to losses*
1825	> *Inconsistent Use of `lastCumulativeRate` in `depositTokens()` and `withdraw()` Functions*
1826	
1827	**Attack the checkpoint on behalf-of paths.** Depositing for another receiver, transferring a position, or having a third party trigger an update frequently sets a timestamp or snapshot without settling what was owed first.
1828	> *Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming*
1829	> *Attackers will reset `avgStart` of any user making rewards stuck for longer and get lost to savings*
1830	> *An attacker may DoS user Fluid balance increases by frontrunning `FluidLocker::claim()` calls and calling `EP_PROGRAM_MANAGER::batchUpdateUserUnits()` directly*
1831	
1832	**Distribute into an empty or stale set.** Rewards queued when supply is zero, an emission period extended after it ended, a sync called at the wrong point in the cycle. Where do those tokens go, and can they be recovered?
1833	> *Lost rewards when the supply is 0, which always happens if rewards are queued before anyone has StakeTracker tokens*
1834	> *Having no deposits in `StakedEXA` will lead to stuck rewards when harvesting*
1835	> *Increasing emissionEnd after the previous emissionEnd ended will yield full rewards according to `newEmissionEnd - prevEmissionEnd`*
1836	> *Wrong reward distribution between early and late depositors because of the late `syncRewards()` call in the cycle*
1837	
1838	**Compare compounding against non-compounding holders.** When a protocol supports both, verify neither systematically drifts against the other.
1839	> *Compounding shares will over time get less rewards than non compounding shares*
1840	
1841	**Vote and claim more than once.** Any per-epoch entitlement — votes, claims, prizes, allocations — needs a consumed flag that survives transfers, re-locks, and epoch boundaries.
1842	> *Voters from VotingEscrow can vote infinite times in `vote_for_gauge_weights()` of GaugeController*
1843	> *Finalize-window vote-changing vulnerability: auto-voters can alter choices post-epoch to manipulate results*
1844	> *Double spending attack in the Vesting contract*
1845	
1846	## Required test
1847	
1848	For each distribution path, write the two-user timeline explicitly: Alice deposits at t0, value V accrues by t1, Bob deposits at t1, distribution happens at t2. Compute what each receives. If Bob receives anything from the t0→t1 accrual, that is the finding — quantify Alice's loss.
1849	
1850	## Every finding needs the timeline
1851	
1852	Two named actors, three timestamps, and the amounts each ends with. Without them it is a LEAD.
1853	# Shared Lens Rules
1854	
1855	## Bundle contents
1856	
1857	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1858	
1859	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1860	
1861	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1862	
1863	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1864	
1865	## Mandatory reasoning protocol
1866	
1867	Four markers. Each has a trigger. When the trigger fires you MUST emit the marker before continuing. Markers live in your working text — they do NOT go inside FINDING/LEAD blocks.
1868	
1869	| Trigger | Marker | Content |
1870	| --- | --- | --- |
1871	| You open a function that moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Explain in plain English what a user gives, what they get, and which totals change. No Solidity jargon — no `safeTransfer`, `mload`, `shares`, `wad`. Where you have to reach for a Solidity term to stay accurate, mark that spot: that is where the bug is. |
1872	| You stop on a line whose purpose is not immediately obvious | `[Why: <file:line>]` | One question that drills past "because that is how it is written." If your answer restates the code, ask again. Stop when the answer exposes the implicit belief the code rests on. |
1873	| A path reads as clean, or a guard looks sufficient | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Three concrete attacker moves against it. Specific addresses, values, and states — never abstractions. |
1874	| You finish a lifecycle from the money map | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | Walk every user withdrawing in the worst order. State explicitly whether the last one gets paid in full, and if not, by how much the protocol is short. |
1875	
1876	Heavy use of these is what produces the audit. Skipping them yields surface-level scanning, which is the failure mode of every junior auditor. The orchestrator checks marker counts.
1877	
1878	## Saturation is mandatory
1879	
1880	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1881	
1882	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1883	
1884	## Do not report
1885	
1886	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1887	
1888	## Output
1889	
1890	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1891	
1892	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1893	
1894	```
1895	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1896	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1897	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1898	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1899	path:
1900	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1901	  2. state changes to Y
1902	  3. actor does Z
1903	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1904	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1905	```
1906	
1907	```
1908	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1909	smell: what you found
1910	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1911	description: one sentence on the trail
1912	```
1913	
1914	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1915	
1916	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.
