1552	# Money Map — raffle.fun (`Raffle` ERC-1167 clone + `RaffleFactory`)
1553	
1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).
1563	
1564	## 1. Assets
1565	| Asset | In | Out |
1566	| --- | --- | --- |
1567	| USDC `quoteToken` (trusted canonical; blacklistable/pausable) | `buyEntries` L224 `safeTransferFrom(msg.sender)`, gross = `entryCount * 1e6` | `redeemWinningTicket` L342 (CashWon → ticket owner), `refundTickets` L369 (→ caller = owner), `releaseSponsorProceeds` L380 (→ `sponsorRecipient`), `releaseProtocolFees` L390 (→ `protocolTreasury`). All via `_transferQuote` (destination-screened) |
1568	| Prize ERC-721 (untrusted contract) | `RaffleFactory::createRaffle` L128 `prize.safeTransferFrom(sponsor, clone)` → `Raffle::onERC721Received` (status → Active) | `redeemWinningTicket` L334 (NftWon → ticket owner; `transferFrom` + `ownerOf` check), `releaseSponsorPrize` L404 (CashWon/Refunding → `sponsorRecipient`; `transferFrom` + `ownerOf` check). NOT destination-screened at release time |
1569	| Native ETH | `requestDraw` `msg.value` | `paidPrice` → VRF wrapper (inside `requestRandomnessPayInNative`); `excess` → `msg.sender` via raw `call(gas())` L267. `receive()` reverts; force-sent ETH has no exit |
1570	| Ticket ERC-721 (this clone's own collection) | minted in `buyEntries` (`_safeMint` → recipient callback) | burned in `refundTickets`, `redeemWinningTicket`. Transferable in EVERY status (DESIGN). `_update` screens `to` via `_isProtocolDestination` |
1571	| Unsolicited USDC / NFTs / ETH | donations | none ("cannot be rescued"); never read by accounting — there is no `balanceOf(this)` anywhere |

1652	# The 0xSimao Method
1653	
1654	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1655	
1656	## The core thesis
1657	
1658	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1659	
1660	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1661	
1662	| Drift | Shape |
1663	| --- | --- |
1664	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1665	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1666	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1667	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1668	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1669	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1670	
1671	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1672	
1673	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1674	
1675	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1676	
1677	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1678	
1679	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1680	
1681	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1682	
1683	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1684	
1685	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1686	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1687	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1688	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1689	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1690	
1691	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1692	
1693	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1694	
1695	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1696	
1697	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1698	
1699	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1700	| --- | --- | --- |
1701	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1702	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1703	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1704	
1705	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1706	
1707	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1708	
1709	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1710	
1711	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1712	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1713	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1714	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1715	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1716	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1717	
1718	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1719	
1720	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1721	
1722	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1723	
1724	Canonical sequences to run:
1725	
1726	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1727	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1728	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1729	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1730	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1731	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1732	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1733	
1734	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1735	
1736	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1737	
1738	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1739	
1740	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1741	
1742	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1743	
1744	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1745	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1746	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1747	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1748	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1749	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1750	
1751	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1752	
1753	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1754	
1755	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1756	
1757	After every finding:
1758	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1759	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1760	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1761	
1762	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1763	
1764	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1765	
1766	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1767	
1768	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1769	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1770	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1771	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1772	
1773	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1774	
1775	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1776	
1777	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1778	
1779	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1780	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1781	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1782	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1783	
1784	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1785	
1786	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1787	
1788	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1789	
1790	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1791	
1792	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1793	
1794	## Do not report
1795	
1796	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1797	# Lens 4 — Liquidation, Bad Debt & Solvency
1798	
1799	You own the machinery that keeps a lending or leverage protocol solvent: health calculations, liquidation eligibility, seize amounts, bonuses, bad-debt clearing, and the interaction between liquidation and every other accounting path.
1800	
1801	Liquidation is where the most accounting variables move at once, under the most adversarial conditions, and it is the path teams test least. It is one of his richest veins.
1802	
1803	## The shape
1804	
1805	Liquidation must (a) be possible whenever the position is unhealthy, (b) be impossible when it is healthy, (c) leave the books balanced afterwards, and (d) actually clear the bad debt it was meant to clear. Break any one and you have either a stuck insolvent position or a profitable attack.
1806	
1807	## Attack surfaces
1808	
1809	**Block the liquidation.** Anything an unhealthy borrower can do to make liquidation revert or become unprofitable is a High — bad debt accrues and the protocol eats it. Look for: paused assets, reverting hooks, dust positions, minimum-debt floors, ordering requirements, gas-unbounded loops, and self-triggerable state that resets a timer.
1810	> *Cannot repay or liquidate on paused asset*
1811	> *Liquidations can be prevented by frontrunning and liquidating 1 debt (or more) due to wrong assumption in POS_MANAGER*
1812	> *Liquidations can be prevented by updating the SL timeout before it expires*
1813	> *`Market::liquidate()` will not work when most of the liquidity is borrowed due to wrong liquidator `transferFrom()` order*
1814	> *Malicious users can DOS the protocol by setting downsideProtected to a large value*
1815	
1816	**Check the health formula against the liquidation formula.** The predicate that says "liquidatable" and the math that executes the liquidation are often written by different people. Verify they agree at the boundary, and that the max liquidatable amount accounts for the bonus — otherwise the position is still unhealthy after a full liquidation.
1817	> *`ViewLogic::maxLiquidatable()` doesn't take the bonus into account, making the agent liquidatable again*
1818	> *Base calculation in `Leverager::isLiquidateable()` is incorrect as the max leverage may be smaller*
1819	> *Contradiction between high-leverage and liquidation check of position*
1820	> *`TARGET_HEALTH` calculation does not consider the adjust factors of the picked seize and repay markets*
1821	> *The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`*
1822	
1823	**Accrue before you judge.** Interest, earnings accumulators, and cumulative rates must be brought current before any health check or liquidation, or positions are judged on stale numbers and liquidations become profitable-but-wrong.
1824	> *Profitable liquidations and accumulation of bad debt due to earnings accumulator not being triggered before liquidating*
1825	> *Market interest is not always accrued*
1826	> *It's possible to borrow, redeem, transfer tokens and exit markets with outdated collateral prices and borrow interest*
1827	> *Liquidating maturities with unassigned earnings will not take into account floating assets increase leading to loss of funds*
1828	
1829	**Follow every variable liquidation touches.** Liquidation moves collateral, debt, insurance, profit, and protocol totals simultaneously. Trace each one and confirm the counterpart update exists. Missing counterparts here are his signature High.
1830	> *Liquidation will reduce total cds deposited amount, leading to incorrect option fees*
1831	> *Type 1 borrower liquidation will incorrectly add cds profit directly to `totalCdsDepositedAmount`*
1832	> *Liquidation profit is never given to cds depositors who will take these losses*
1833	> *Some liquidated collateral will be locked*
1834	> *Missing Update to `omnichain.totalAvailableLiquidationAmount` in `withdrawUser`*
1835	
1836	**Verify bad debt actually clears.** A clearing function that leaves dust, or that only works on the last maturity, or that leaves unassigned earnings claimable by anyone, means insolvency accumulates silently.
1837	> *Liquidations will leave dust when repaying expired maturities, making it impossible to clear bad debt putting the protocol at a risk of insolvency*
1838	> *Some bad debt will not be cleared when it should which will cause accrual of bad debt decreasing the protocol's solvency*
1839	> *Liquidator will leave a pool with unassigned earnings on `Market::clearBadDebt()` free to claim for anyone when the repaid maturity is not the last*
1840	> *Bad debt is never handled which places insolvency risks on BendDAO*
1841	
1842	**Cap the price and the seize.** Unbounded liquidation prices, unprioritized collateral selection, and missing slippage on the liquidator's swap all leak value.
1843	> *Major insolvency risk in `LiquidationLogic::executeCrossLiquidateERC721()` due to not setting a maximum liquidation price*
1844	> *Liquidation does not prioritize lowest LTV tokens*
1845	> *Liquidations miss delegate call to swapper*
1846	> *Lack of slippage protection leads to loss of protocol funds*
1847	
1848	**Probe the leverage-adjustment boundary.** Increase/decrease leverage, partial repay, and position adjustment paths must respect minimum debt, maximum debt, and fees. They routinely do not.
1849	> *`ManagedLeveragedVault::decreaseLeverage()` will not work when it goes below the minimum debt*
1850	> *`ManagedLeveragedVault::executeWithdrawalEpoch()` incorrect ICR and DoSed withdrawals due to not accounting for fees*
1851	> *DoSed withdrawals due to `ManagedLeveragedVault::executeWithdrawalEpoch()` repaying debt above limit*
1852	
1853	## Every finding needs the position
1854	
1855	Give the concrete position: collateral amount, debt amount, price, resulting health factor before and after. State whether the protocol is left short and by how much.
1856	# Shared Lens Rules
1857	
1858	## Bundle contents
1859	
1860	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1861	
1862	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1863	
1864	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1865	
1866	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1867	
1868	## Mandatory reasoning protocol
1869	
1870	Four markers. Each has a trigger. When the trigger fires you MUST emit the marker before continuing. Markers live in your working text — they do NOT go inside FINDING/LEAD blocks.
1871	
1872	| Trigger | Marker | Content |
1873	| --- | --- | --- |
1874	| You open a function that moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Explain in plain English what a user gives, what they get, and which totals change. No Solidity jargon — no `safeTransfer`, `mload`, `shares`, `wad`. Where you have to reach for a Solidity term to stay accurate, mark that spot: that is where the bug is. |
1875	| You stop on a line whose purpose is not immediately obvious | `[Why: <file:line>]` | One question that drills past "because that is how it is written." If your answer restates the code, ask again. Stop when the answer exposes the implicit belief the code rests on. |
1876	| A path reads as clean, or a guard looks sufficient | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Three concrete attacker moves against it. Specific addresses, values, and states — never abstractions. |
1877	| You finish a lifecycle from the money map | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | Walk every user withdrawing in the worst order. State explicitly whether the last one gets paid in full, and if not, by how much the protocol is short. |
1878	
1879	Heavy use of these is what produces the audit. Skipping them yields surface-level scanning, which is the failure mode of every junior auditor. The orchestrator checks marker counts.
1880	
1881	## Saturation is mandatory
1882	
1883	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1884	
1885	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1886	
1887	## Do not report
1888	
1889	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1890	
1891	## Output
1892	
1893	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1894	
1895	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1896	
1897	```
1898	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1899	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1900	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1901	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1902	path:
1903	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1904	  2. state changes to Y
1905	  3. actor does Z
1906	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1907	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1908	```
1909	
1910	```
1911	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1912	smell: what you found
1913	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1914	description: one sentence on the trail
1915	```
1916	
1917	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1918	
1919	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.

1552	# Money Map — raffle.fun (`Raffle` ERC-1167 clone + `RaffleFactory`)
1553	
1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).

1649	- Untrusted callouts: prize `transferFrom` / `ownerOf` / `safeTransferFrom` / `supportsInterface`; recipient `onERC721Received` (`_safeMint`, ticket `safeTransferFrom`); requester ETH `call(gas())` (after `vrfRequestId` is set, before the event). Factory views `raffleImplementation()` / `isRaffle()` are called from every `_update` and `_transferQuote`.
1650	- Constants: ENTRY_PRICE 1e6; fee 500 bps; cash 8000 bps; refund batch ≤ 100 tickets; sale ≤ 30 d; request window 2 d; callback window 2 d; callback gas 300k; 30 confirmations.
1651	- Dependency sources present under `packages/contracts/node_modules/` (OZ 5.6.1, Chainlink 1.5.0 `VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase`, `IVRFV2PlusWrapper`). The wrapper implementation itself is not vendored — reason from the trusted canonical VRF v2.5 wrapper.
1652	# The 0xSimao Method
1653	
1654	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1655	
1656	## The core thesis
1657	
1658	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1659	
1660	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1661	
1662	| Drift | Shape |
1663	| --- | --- |
1664	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1665	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1666	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1667	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1668	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1669	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1670	
1671	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1672	
1673	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1674	
1675	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1676	
1677	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1678	
1679	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1680	
1681	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1682	
1683	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1684	
1685	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1686	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1687	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1688	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1689	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1690	
1691	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1692	
1693	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1694	
1695	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1696	
1697	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1698	
1699	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1700	| --- | --- | --- |
1701	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1702	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1703	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1704	
1705	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1706	
1707	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1708	
1709	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1710	
1711	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1712	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1713	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1714	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1715	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1716	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1717	
1718	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1719	
1720	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1721	
1722	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1723	
1724	Canonical sequences to run:
1725	
1726	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1727	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1728	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1729	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1730	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1731	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1732	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1733	
1734	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1735	
1736	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1737	
1738	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1739	
1740	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1741	
1742	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1743	
1744	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1745	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1746	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1747	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1748	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1749	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1750	
1751	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1752	
1753	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1754	
1755	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1756	
1757	After every finding:
1758	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1759	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1760	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1761	
1762	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1763	
1764	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1765	
1766	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1767	
1768	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1769	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1770	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1771	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1772	
1773	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1774	
1775	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1776	
1777	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1778	
1779	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1780	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1781	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1782	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1783	
1784	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1785	
1786	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1787	
1788	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1789	
1790	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1791	
1792	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1793	
1794	## Do not report
1795	
1796	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1797	# Lens 5 — Cross-Chain & Asynchronous State
1798	
1799	You own every message that crosses a trust or latency boundary: LayerZero, CCIP, Connext, native bridges, and any request/callback pair where state is written on one side and read on the other.
1800	
1801	If the protocol is single-chain and fully synchronous, say so explicitly and spend your effort on the request/callback and escrow paths instead — the same failure modes appear wherever an action is split across two transactions.
1802	
1803	## The shape
1804	
1805	Two chains hold copies of a "global" state. Messages are asynchronous, can arrive out of order, can fail, and can be sent by anyone with the right payload. Any design that treats the remote write as immediate, ordered, or atomic with the local write is broken — and the resulting desync is permanent because there is no path that reconciles it.
1806	
1807	## Attack surfaces
1808	
1809	**Non-atomic global state.** The core LayerZero/CCIP failure: chain A updates a global aggregate and sends it to chain B, while chain B does the same. Whichever message lands last overwrites the other's update, silently destroying it.
1810	> *Using LayerZero for synchronizing global states between two chains may lead to overwriting of global states*
1811	> *`borrowing::liquidate()` sends the wrong liquidation index to the destination chain, overwriting liquidation information and getting collateral stuck*
1812	> *Cds amounts to reduce from each chain are incorrect and will lead to the inability to withdraw cds in one of the chains*
1813	
1814	**Value debited here, credited nowhere.** If the destination handler can revert — for any reason, including gas, a paused token, a blacklist, or an unset peer — the source funds are already gone. Enumerate every revert in the receive path and ask what happens to the debited amount.
1815	> *Exercise option cross chain message in the (m)TapiocaOFT will always revert in the destination, losing debited funds in the source chain*
1816	> *Users will lock raffle prizes on the `WinnablesPrizeManager` contract by calling `WinnablesTicketManager::propagateRaffleWinner` with wrong CCIP inputs*
1817	> *Attacker can block LayerZero channel due to missing check of minimum gas passed*
1818	> *Send should revert if the gas limit has not been set for a destination chain (peer)*
1819	
1820	**Unvalidated message parameters.** The payload is attacker-controlled unless proven otherwise. Check the sender, the source chain, the peer registration, the recipient, and every amount/share field independently — a mismatch between an amount field and a shares field is a classic drain.
1821	> *All assets of (m)TapiocaOFT can be stolen by depositing to strategy cross chain call with 1 amount but maximum shares possible*
1822	> *TOFT in (m)TapiocaOft contracts can be stolen by calling `removeCollateral()` with a malicious `removeParams.market`*
1823	> *`triggerSendFrom()` will send all the ETH in the destination chain to the `refundAddress` in the LzCallParams argument*
1824	> *NFTs can be stolen by calling `send()` and receiving the nfts in another chain*
1825	
1826	**Address assumptions across chains.** The same address is not the same entity on every chain. Smart wallets, contracts deployed with different nonces, and CREATE2 with different init code all break the "send to msg.sender on the other side" pattern.
1827	> *Lost nfts due to smart wallets having different addresses on different chains*
1828	> *AaveETHYieldBackend uses wrong WETH address for Polygon (returns WETH instead of WPOL)*
1829	
1830	**Fees and gas asymmetry.** Fees quoted on the source chain rarely equal costs on the destination. Charging symmetric fees, hardcoding gas limits, or forgetting to forward `msg.value` for the message fee all fail.
1831	> *`GlobalVariables::oftOrCollateralReceiveFromOtherChains()` calculates the fee as if it was the same in both chains, which is false*
1832	> *`GlobalVariables::oftOrCollateralReceiveFromOtherChains()` always charges twice the collateral on `COLLATERAL_TRANSFER`, which is not needed*
1833	> *mTapiocaOFT can't be rebalanced because the Balancer calls `swapETH()` or `swap()` of the RouterETH but does not forward ether for the message fee*
1834	> *BlsBn254 is not available in certain chains due to hardcoded gas limit*
1835	
1836	**Yield and collateral on the wrong chain.** When a protocol tracks positions on one chain and assets on another, verify every update lands where the asset actually is.
1837	> *`treasury.updateYieldsFromLiquidatedLrts()` updates the yield in the current chain, but collateral may be in the other chain*
1838	
1839	**Callbacks and retries.** Failed-message retry paths, `executeFailedWithUpdatedArgs`, and generic callback handlers are entry points with the weakest validation in the codebase. Treat them as fully permissionless until proven otherwise, and check for reentrancy into the main accounting.
1840	> *ConnextHandler `executeFailedWithUpdatedArgs(...)` reentrancy allowedCaller can steal all ConnextHandler tokens*
1841	> *Funds may be stolen by calling `onMoreFlashLoan()` directly*
1842	> *In BaseRouter, the beneficiary isn't checked when starting a flashloan action and it replaces the previous beneficiary*
1843	
1844	**Self-destruct and upgrade exposure on proxied modules.** Module contracts reached by delegatecall inherit the caller's storage and can be destroyed or reinitialized.
1845	> *TOFT and USDO Modules Can Be Selfdestructed*
1846	
1847	## Every finding needs the two-chain trace
1848	
1849	State the ordering explicitly: what chain A does, what chain B does, in which order the messages land, and what the two states are afterwards. Name the value that is now unrecoverable.
1850	# Shared Lens Rules
1851	
1852	## Bundle contents
1853	
1854	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1855	
1856	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1857	
1858	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1859	
1860	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1861	
1862	## Mandatory reasoning protocol
1863	
1864	Four markers. Each has a trigger. When the trigger fires you MUST emit the marker before continuing. Markers live in your working text — they do NOT go inside FINDING/LEAD blocks.
1865	
1866	| Trigger | Marker | Content |
1867	| --- | --- | --- |
1868	| You open a function that moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Explain in plain English what a user gives, what they get, and which totals change. No Solidity jargon — no `safeTransfer`, `mload`, `shares`, `wad`. Where you have to reach for a Solidity term to stay accurate, mark that spot: that is where the bug is. |
1869	| You stop on a line whose purpose is not immediately obvious | `[Why: <file:line>]` | One question that drills past "because that is how it is written." If your answer restates the code, ask again. Stop when the answer exposes the implicit belief the code rests on. |
1870	| A path reads as clean, or a guard looks sufficient | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Three concrete attacker moves against it. Specific addresses, values, and states — never abstractions. |
1871	| You finish a lifecycle from the money map | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | Walk every user withdrawing in the worst order. State explicitly whether the last one gets paid in full, and if not, by how much the protocol is short. |
1872	
1873	Heavy use of these is what produces the audit. Skipping them yields surface-level scanning, which is the failure mode of every junior auditor. The orchestrator checks marker counts.
1874	
1875	## Saturation is mandatory
1876	
1877	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1878	
1879	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1880	
1881	## Do not report
1882	
1883	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1884	
1885	## Output
1886	
1887	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1888	
1889	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1890	
1891	```
1892	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1893	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1894	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1895	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1896	path:
1897	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1898	  2. state changes to Y
1899	  3. actor does Z
1900	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1901	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1902	```
1903	
1904	```
1905	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1906	smell: what you found
1907	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1908	description: one sentence on the trail
1909	```
1910	
1911	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1912	
1913	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.

1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).

1652	# The 0xSimao Method
1653	
1654	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1655	
1656	## The core thesis
1657	
1658	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1659	
1660	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1661	
1662	| Drift | Shape |
1663	| --- | --- |
1664	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1665	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1666	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1667	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1668	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1669	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1670	
1671	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1672	
1673	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1674	
1675	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1676	
1677	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1678	
1679	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1680	
1681	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1682	
1683	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1684	
1685	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1686	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1687	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1688	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1689	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1690	
1691	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1692	
1693	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1694	
1695	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1696	
1697	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1698	
1699	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1700	| --- | --- | --- |
1701	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1702	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1703	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1704	
1705	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1706	
1707	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1708	
1709	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1710	
1711	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1712	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1713	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1714	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1715	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1716	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1717	
1718	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1719	
1720	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1721	
1722	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1723	
1724	Canonical sequences to run:
1725	
1726	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1727	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1728	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1729	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1730	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1731	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1732	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1733	
1734	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1735	
1736	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1737	
1738	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1739	
1740	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1741	
1742	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1743	
1744	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1745	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1746	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1747	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1748	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1749	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1750	
1751	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1752	
1753	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1754	
1755	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1756	
1757	After every finding:
1758	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1759	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1760	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1761	
1762	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1763	
1764	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1765	
1766	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1767	
1768	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1769	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1770	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1771	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1772	
1773	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1774	
1775	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1776	
1777	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1778	
1779	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1780	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1781	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1782	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1783	
1784	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1785	
1786	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1787	
1788	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1789	
1790	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1791	
1792	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1793	
1794	## Do not report
1795	
1796	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1797	# Lens 6 — Rounding, Precision & Scale
1798	
1799	You own integer arithmetic: rounding direction, truncation, decimals, fixed-point scale, casts, and overflow. Every division is a decision about who absorbs the remainder, and every decision made in the wrong direction is extractable.
1800	
1801	0xSimao's framing is sharper than "there is precision loss": he asks **which party the rounding favors, whether that favoring can be repeated, and whether it compounds.** A rounding error that a user can trigger in a loop is a drain, not a nit.
1802	
1803	## Attack surfaces
1804	
1805	**Establish the correct direction, then check every division.** Deposits round shares DOWN. Withdrawals round assets DOWN. Debt rounds UP. Fees round UP. Anything favoring the user in a repeatable path is extractable; anything favoring the protocol in a *forced* path can be weaponized as griefing or, when the protocol is a counterparty to itself, as a drain.
1806	> *Wrong rounding direction in `StakingPool::unstake()` can be abused*
1807	> *The Rounding Done in Protocol's Favor Can Be Weaponized to Drain the Protocol*
1808	> *Aave rounding behavior allows malicious users to drain accumulated yield via small withdrawals*
1809	> *`TradingLimits::update()` incorrectly only rounds up when `deltaFlowUnits` becomes 0, which will silently increase trading limits*
1810	
1811	**Find division before multiplication.** `a / b * c` truncates early and amplifies the loss. Trace across function boundaries too — a truncated return value multiplied by the caller is the same bug spread over two files. `mulDiv` exists for this; note its absence.
1812	> *`FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPercentage()` divides before multiplying, suffering a significant precision error*
1813	> *`LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart` does not use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts, possibly leading to DoS or loss of funds*
1814	
1815	**Drive results to zero.** Feed 1 wei, 1 share, and 1 second into every calculation. Where do fees truncate to zero? Where does interest accrue nothing? Where does a reward rate become zero and lock the stream permanently? Zero results flip formulas and are frequently permanent.
1816	> *Integer Truncation in Incentive Rate Permanently Locks Unstreamed Rewards*
1817	> *Precision Loss in `notifyRewardAmount` Function Causes Unclaimable RewardToken*
1818	> *Significant rounding errors due to `gameETH` not having precision*
1819	> *Estimated prize draws in TieredLiquidityDistributor are off due to rounding down when calculating the sum, leading to incorrect prizes*
1820	
1821	**Check every decimal assumption.** Hardcoded `1e18` against a 6-decimal token. `18 - decimals` underflowing for >18-decimal tokens. Oracle decimals assumed constant when the feed sets them. A price feed returning 8 decimals fed into 18-decimal math.
1822	> *Decimals of LendingPool don't take into account the offset introduced by VIRTUAL_SHARES*
1823	> *WBTCZapper decimal mismatch causes revert*
1824	> *WBTCZapper precision loss will lead to reverts*
1825	> *`PreDepositVault` does not collect interest for `WBTC`*
1826	
1827	**Overflow the intermediate.** For every `a * b / c`, construct inputs where `a * b` exceeds uint256 before the division rescues it. Uniswap `sqrtPriceX96` math is the classic: squaring it directly overflows for real pools.
1828	> *Performing a direct multiplication in `_getPriceFromSqrtX96` will overflow for some uniswap pools*
1829	
1830	**Break the casts.** `uint256 → uint128/96/64` without a bounds check. Signed/unsigned round trips that drop the sign bit and turn a small negative into an enormous positive. Unsigned subtraction where the operands are not provably ordered.
1831	> *Potential Underflow in `withdrawInterest`*
1832	> *DOS on liquidation type 1 due to underflow in cds profits computation*
1833	> *`state.cumulativeDepositsMultiplierX18` may become 0 or negative, leading to loss of funds*
1834	> *API3 oracle timestamp can be set to future timestamp and block API3 Oracle usage to make code revert in underflow*
1835	
1836	**Check the units of every constant.** A bare number where a time unit belongs is a whole-order-of-magnitude bug and reads as innocuous.
1837	> *`FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPercentage()` uses 540 instead of `540 days` leading to stuck funds as the unlocking percentage will be bigger than `100%` and underflow*
1838	> *`FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPercentage()` incorrectly divides one of the components of the formula by `S`, leading to always having `80%` penalty*
1839	
1840	**Divide by an unconstrained value.** `x / tickSpacing`, `x / totalSupply`, `x / config.value` — construct the input that drives the divisor to zero or one.
1841	
1842	## Every finding needs concrete arithmetic
1843	
1844	Walk the numbers. State the inputs, the intermediate values, the result, and the correct result. Then state the extraction per call and whether it can be looped. Without numbers it is a LEAD, no exceptions.
1845	# Shared Lens Rules
1846	
1847	## Bundle contents
1848	
1849	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1850	
1851	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1852	
1853	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1854	
1855	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1856	
1857	## Mandatory reasoning protocol
1858	
1859	Four markers. Each has a trigger. When the trigger fires you MUST emit the marker before continuing. Markers live in your working text — they do NOT go inside FINDING/LEAD blocks.
1860	
1861	| Trigger | Marker | Content |
1862	| --- | --- | --- |
1863	| You open a function that moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Explain in plain English what a user gives, what they get, and which totals change. No Solidity jargon — no `safeTransfer`, `mload`, `shares`, `wad`. Where you have to reach for a Solidity term to stay accurate, mark that spot: that is where the bug is. |
1864	| You stop on a line whose purpose is not immediately obvious | `[Why: <file:line>]` | One question that drills past "because that is how it is written." If your answer restates the code, ask again. Stop when the answer exposes the implicit belief the code rests on. |
1865	| A path reads as clean, or a guard looks sufficient | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Three concrete attacker moves against it. Specific addresses, values, and states — never abstractions. |
1866	| You finish a lifecycle from the money map | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | Walk every user withdrawing in the worst order. State explicitly whether the last one gets paid in full, and if not, by how much the protocol is short. |
1867	
1868	Heavy use of these is what produces the audit. Skipping them yields surface-level scanning, which is the failure mode of every junior auditor. The orchestrator checks marker counts.
1869	
1870	## Saturation is mandatory
1871	
1872	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1873	
1874	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1875	
1876	## Do not report
1877	
1878	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1879	
1880	## Output
1881	
1882	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1883	
1884	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1885	
1886	```
1887	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1888	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1889	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1890	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1891	path:
1892	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1893	  2. state changes to Y
1894	  3. actor does Z
1895	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1896	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1897	```
1898	
1899	```
1900	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1901	smell: what you found
1902	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1903	description: one sentence on the trail
1904	```
1905	
1906	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1907	
1908	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.
1909
