1552	# Money Map — raffle.fun (`Raffle` ERC-1167 clone + `RaffleFactory`)
1553	
1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).
1563	
1564	## 1. Assets
1565	| Asset | In | Out |
1566	| --- | --- | --- |
1567	| USDC `quoteToken` (trusted canonical; blacklistable/pausable) | `buyEntries` L224 `safeTransferFrom(msg.sender)`, gross = `entryCount * 1e6` | `redeemWinningTicket` L342 (CashWon → ticket owner), `refundTickets` L369 (→ caller = owner), `releaseSponsorProceeds` L380 (→ `sponsorRecipient`), `releaseProtocolFees` L390 (→ `protocolTreasury`). All via `_transferQuote` (destination-screened) |
1568	| Prize ERC-721 (untrusted contract) | `RaffleFactory::createRaffle` L128 `prize.safeTransferFrom(sponsor, clone)` → `Raffle::onERC721Received` (status → Active) | `redeemWinningTicket` L334 (NftWon → ticket owner; `transferFrom` + `ownerOf` check), `releaseSponsorPrize` L404 (CashWon/Refunding → `sponsorRecipient`; `transferFrom` + `ownerOf` check). NOT destination-screened at release time |
1569	| Native ETH | `requestDraw` `msg.value` | `paidPrice` → VRF wrapper (inside `requestRandomnessPayInNative`); `excess` → `msg.sender` via raw `call(gas())` L267. `receive()` reverts; force-sent ETH has no exit |
1570	| Ticket ERC-721 (this clone's own collection) | minted in `buyEntries` (`_safeMint` → recipient callback) | burned in `refundTickets`, `redeemWinningTicket`. Transferable in EVERY status (DESIGN). `_update` screens `to` via `_isProtocolDestination` |
1571	| Unsolicited USDC / NFTs / ETH | donations | none ("cannot be rescued"); never read by accounting — there is no `balanceOf(this)` anywhere |

1652	# The 0xSimao Method
1653	
1654	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1655	
1656	## The core thesis
1657	
1658	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1659	
1660	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1661	
1662	| Drift | Shape |
1663	| --- | --- |
1664	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1665	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1666	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1667	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1668	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1669	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1670	
1671	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1672	
1673	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1674	
1675	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1676	
1677	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1678	
1679	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1680	
1681	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1682	
1683	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1684	
1685	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1686	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1687	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1688	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1689	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1690	
1691	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1692	
1693	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1694	
1695	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1696	
1697	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1698	
1699	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1700	| --- | --- | --- |
1701	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1702	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1703	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1704	
1705	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1706	
1707	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1708	
1709	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1710	
1711	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1712	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1713	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1714	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1715	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1716	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1717	
1718	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1719	
1720	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1721	
1722	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1723	
1724	Canonical sequences to run:
1725	
1726	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1727	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1728	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1729	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1730	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1731	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1732	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1733	
1734	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1735	
1736	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1737	
1738	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1739	
1740	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1741	
1742	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1743	
1744	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1745	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1746	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1747	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1748	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1749	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1750	
1751	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1752	
1753	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1754	
1755	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1756	
1757	After every finding:
1758	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1759	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1760	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1761	
1762	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1763	
1764	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1765	
1766	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1767	
1768	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1769	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1770	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1771	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1772	
1773	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1774	
1775	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1776	
1777	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1778	
1779	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1780	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1781	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1782	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1783	
1784	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1785	
1786	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1787	
1788	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1789	
1790	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1791	
1792	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1793	
1794	## Do not report
1795	
1796	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1797	# Lens 7 — Ordering, MEV & Price Manipulation
1798	
1799	You own everything that depends on *when* a transaction lands relative to others: frontrunning, sandwiching, initialization races, oracle reads, and arbitrage against discrete state changes.
1800	
1801	The bar matters here. Ordinary slippage on a swap a user chose is not a finding. What you are hunting is (a) protocol-owned value exposed to MEV without protection, (b) a state change large enough to arbitrage, and (c) a one-shot action anyone can win.
1802	
1803	## Attack surfaces
1804	
1805	**Win the initialization race.** Any `initialize`, first-deposit, pool-creation, or set-once function callable by anyone before the deployer gets there. These are consistently High: an arbitrary initial price or an attacker-owned proxy is total loss.
1806	> *Uniswap v4 pool initialization can be frontrunned, setting an arbitrary price, and stealing tokens*
1807	> *`BoldToken` initialization can be frontrun to silently mint/approve bold to an attacker*
1808	> *Missing `__Ownable_init()` call in `LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart::initialize()`*
1809	> *`Codeup::claimCodeupERC20()` may be forever DoSed by creating the `Uniswap` pool before it is called*
1810	
1811	**Find protocol-owned swaps with no protection.** A permissionless function that swaps protocol funds with `amountOutMin = 0` or `deadline = block.timestamp` is free money for a sandwicher, and the protocol — not a consenting user — pays.
1812	> *Distribute is permissionless, allowing malicious users to specify 0 slippage and sandwich the swap*
1813	> *Swapping with deadline as `block.timestamp` and 0 minimum amount out is vulnerable to MEV*
1814	> *`UniswapV2Swapper` uses `block.timestamp` for deadline*
1815	> *`_addLiquidity()` slippage is incorrectly set*
1816	> *Lack of deadline in `PowerToken.buy` can lead to user's cashToken being distributed through ZeroToken holders*
1817	
1818	**Arbitrage the discrete jump.** Any transaction that steps a rate, TVL, price, or reserve discontinuously can be front-run on one side and back-run on the other. Look for admin rate updates, reward top-ups, rebalances, and TVL syncs.
1819	> *`increaseNetworkTotal()` allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction*
1820	> *Withdrawals logic allows MEV exploits of TVL changes and zero-slippage zero-fee swaps*
1821	> *`_rebalanceWithdraw()` mechanism in glAVAX allows arbitrage opportunities by changing the shares/AVAX ratio*
1822	> *Price formula in `TpdaLiquidationPair._computePrice()` does not account for a jump in liquidatable balance*
1823	> *Drained oracle fees from market by depositing and withdrawing immediately without triggering settlement fees*
1824	
1825	**Read the manipulable price.** `slot0`, spot reserves, and any vault rate derived from a live balance are manipulable within a single transaction. Distinguish a genuine TWAP from a spot read dressed as one, and check which price the protocol picks when several are available.
1826	> *Strategy main ticks are set according to the tick in `slot0`, leading to incorrect allocation and loss of funds*
1827	> *`LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart` picks the wrong Uniswap price, allowing borrowing at a discount by swapping before withdrawing*
1828	> *Interest rate in `LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart` may be easily manipulated by depositing, taking a loan and withdrawing*
1829	> *`PHyperLPoolSwapInside::_rebalance()` checks the price manipulation before and after the swap with the same price threshold*
1830	> *Locker owners can leverage low liquidity pools to bypass the tax mechanism*
1831	
1832	**Front-run for grief, not profit.** Cancelling a raffle before it starts, claiming a one-shot right, resetting someone's timer, or triggering a state transition to block another user. Cost to the attacker is often near zero.
1833	> *Attacker will prevent any raffles by calling `WinnablesTicketManager::cancelRaffle` before admin starts raffle*
1834	> *Malicious user may frontrun `GoodDollarExpansionController::mintUBIFromReserveBalance()` to make protocol funds stuck*
1835	> *Anyone can frontrun a relayer interaction with the same arguments but a much higher/lower relayer fee*
1836	> *Anyone will DoS setting a new rewards duration which harms the protocol/users*
1837	
1838	**Break the approval window.** Functions taking shares (rather than assets) as an argument, or relying on a prior approval, can be made to revert or over-spend if state moves between approval and execution.
1839	> *`repay()`, `liquidate()` and `liquidateWLp()` receive shares as argument, which may revert if from approval to tx settled blocks have passed*
1840	> *`safeApprove(...)` reverts if approval is different than 0, use `safeIncreaseAllowance(...)` instead*
1841	> *`FlashRolloverLoan_G5` will not work for certain tokens due to not setting the approval to `0` after repaying a loan*
1842	
1843	**Replay the signature.** Missing nonce, missing deadline, missing chain id, zero timestamp accepted, or parameters excluded from the signed digest so an attacker can pair a valid signature with hostile arguments.
1844	> *Validator signature with zero timestamp can always be replayed*
1845	> *Signature Replay attack possible on `updateWorkerDeploymentConfigWithSig()` in Blueprintcore.sol which leads to users losing funds*
1846	> *Signatures missing some parameters being vulnerable to attackers using them coupled with malicious parameters*
1847	> *All curve params should be signed by the schnorr private key in the proof, or users may be griefed*
1848	
1849	## Every finding needs the ordering
1850	
1851	State the transaction sequence explicitly: attacker tx, victim tx, attacker tx. Give the attacker's cost and profit. If the attack is a grief, state the cost to the attacker (often zero) and the damage to the victim.
1852	# Shared Lens Rules
1853	
1854	## Bundle contents
1855	
1856	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1857	
1858	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1859	
1860	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1861	
1862	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1863	
1864	## Mandatory reasoning protocol
1865	
1866	Four markers. Each has a trigger. When the trigger fires you MUST emit the marker before continuing. Markers live in your working text — they do NOT go inside FINDING/LEAD blocks.
1867	
1868	| Trigger | Marker | Content |
1869	| --- | --- | --- |
1870	| You open a function that moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Explain in plain English what a user gives, what they get, and which totals change. No Solidity jargon — no `safeTransfer`, `mload`, `shares`, `wad`. Where you have to reach for a Solidity term to stay accurate, mark that spot: that is where the bug is. |
1871	| You stop on a line whose purpose is not immediately obvious | `[Why: <file:line>]` | One question that drills past "because that is how it is written." If your answer restates the code, ask again. Stop when the answer exposes the implicit belief the code rests on. |
1872	| A path reads as clean, or a guard looks sufficient | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Three concrete attacker moves against it. Specific addresses, values, and states — never abstractions. |
1873	| You finish a lifecycle from the money map | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | Walk every user withdrawing in the worst order. State explicitly whether the last one gets paid in full, and if not, by how much the protocol is short. |
1874	
1875	Heavy use of these is what produces the audit. Skipping them yields surface-level scanning, which is the failure mode of every junior auditor. The orchestrator checks marker counts.
1876	
1877	## Saturation is mandatory
1878	
1879	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1880	
1881	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1882	
1883	## Do not report
1884	
1885	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1886	
1887	## Output
1888	
1889	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1890	
1891	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1892	
1893	```
1894	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1895	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1896	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1897	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1898	path:
1899	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1900	  2. state changes to Y
1901	  3. actor does Z
1902	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1903	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1904	```
1905	
1906	```
1907	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1908	smell: what you found
1909	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1910	description: one sentence on the trail
1911	```
1912	
1913	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1914	
1915	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.

1552	# Money Map — raffle.fun (`Raffle` ERC-1167 clone + `RaffleFactory`)
1553	
1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).

1647	- `nonReentrant`: `buyEntries`, `requestDraw`, `enableRefunds`, `settleWinningTicket`, `redeemWinningTicket`, `refundTickets`, `releaseSponsorProceeds`, `releaseProtocolFees`, `releaseSponsorPrize`; factory `createRaffle`. (OZ 5.6.1 guard uses an ERC-7201 slot; clone starts at 0 ≠ ENTERED, so it works without a constructor.)
1648	- Unguarded: ticket `transferFrom` / `safeTransferFrom` / `approve` / `setApprovalForAll`, `onERC721Received`, `rawFulfillRandomWords` (wrapper-only), inherited `getBalance` / `getLinkToken`, views.
1649	- Untrusted callouts: prize `transferFrom` / `ownerOf` / `safeTransferFrom` / `supportsInterface`; recipient `onERC721Received` (`_safeMint`, ticket `safeTransferFrom`); requester ETH `call(gas())` (after `vrfRequestId` is set, before the event). Factory views `raffleImplementation()` / `isRaffle()` are called from every `_update` and `_transferQuote`.
1650	- Constants: ENTRY_PRICE 1e6; fee 500 bps; cash 8000 bps; refund batch ≤ 100 tickets; sale ≤ 30 d; request window 2 d; callback window 2 d; callback gas 300k; 30 confirmations.
1651	- Dependency sources present under `packages/contracts/node_modules/` (OZ 5.6.1, Chainlink 1.5.0 `VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase`, `IVRFV2PlusWrapper`). The wrapper implementation itself is not vendored — reason from the trusted canonical VRF v2.5 wrapper.
1652	# The 0xSimao Method
1653	
1654	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1655	
1656	## The core thesis
1657	
1658	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1659	
1660	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1661	
1662	| Drift | Shape |
1663	| --- | --- |
1664	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1665	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1666	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1667	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1668	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1669	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1670	
1671	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1672	
1673	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1674	
1675	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1676	
1677	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1678	
1679	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1680	
1681	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1682	
1683	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1684	
1685	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1686	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1687	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1688	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1689	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1690	
1691	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1692	
1693	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1694	
1695	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1696	
1697	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1698	
1699	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1700	| --- | --- | --- |
1701	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1702	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1703	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1704	
1705	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1706	
1707	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1708	
1709	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1710	
1711	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1712	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1713	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1714	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1715	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1716	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1717	
1718	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1719	
1720	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1721	
1722	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1723	
1724	Canonical sequences to run:
1725	
1726	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1727	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1728	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1729	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1730	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1731	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1732	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1733	
1734	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1735	
1736	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1737	
1738	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1739	
1740	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1741	
1742	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1743	
1744	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1745	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1746	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1747	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1748	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1749	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1750	
1751	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1752	
1753	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1754	
1755	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1756	
1757	After every finding:
1758	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1759	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1760	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1761	
1762	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1763	
1764	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1765	
1766	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1767	
1768	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1769	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1770	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1771	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1772	
1773	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1774	
1775	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1776	
1777	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1778	
1779	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1780	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1781	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1782	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1783	
1784	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1785	
1786	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1787	
1788	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1789	
1790	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1791	
1792	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1793	
1794	## Do not report
1795	
1796	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1797	# Lens 8 — Denial of Service & Griefing
1798	
1799	You own availability. Your target is not "this could revert" — it is **a permanent or long-lived block on a function that must remain available, reachable by an attacker at low cost, with a real cost to someone else.**
1800	
1801	The severity ladder that matters: funds permanently stuck > liquidations blocked (because bad debt accrues) > withdrawals blocked for a bounded period > core function unusable > admin function unusable.
1802	
1803	## Attack surfaces
1804	
1805	**Grow an unbounded array.** Any loop over a user-extendable structure — queues, pending removals, request lists, holder arrays, market lists — is an out-of-gas bomb if anyone can append cheaply. Ask for the batch parameter; note its absence.
1806	> *DoSed `Voter::finalize()` due to unbounded pending removals lacking a batch argument variable*
1807	> *`BatchOut::withdrawFulfill()` can be DoSed by spamming withdrawal requests, leading to OOG reverts*
1808	> *`Treasury.noOfBorrowers` can be set to 0 by looping wei deposit<->withdrawals and DoS withdrawals and reset borrower debt*
1809	
1810	**Poison one element of a batch.** A single reverting item in a loop that reverts the whole transaction. Reverting hooks, blacklisted recipients, zero-transfer-reverting tokens, and `address(0)` entries are all cheap to inject.
1811	> *Halted withdrawals in BatchOut due to setting `withdrawTo` to `address(0)` in `scheduleWithdrawal()`*
1812	> *Scheduled withdrawals with unsupported tokens will be halted*
1813	> *`Claimers` can receive less `feePerClaim` than they should if some prizes are already claimed or if reverts because of a reverting hook*
1814	> *If wLP is blacklisted, then user will not be able to withdraw it*
1815	> *Gas Manipulation by Malicious Winners in `claimPrizes` Function*
1816	
1817	**Exhaust a shared resource.** Buffers, caps, queues, and limits that any user can fill to lock everyone else out.
1818	> *DOS of `completeQueuedWithdrawal` when ERC20 buffer is filled*
1819	> *Attacker can DoS user withdrawals at no cost*
1820	> *Anyone can grief users, stopping them from fulfilling their withdrawals*
1821	> *Worker-Induced Denial-of-Service in Deployment Requests Due to Lack of a Cancellation Mechanism*
1822	
1823	**Make the internal call impossible.** A function that internally deposits, withdraws, harvests, or rebalances will inherit every failure mode of the thing it calls. Full utilization, paused markets, frozen assets, and reverting receive hooks all propagate up into a core path that looks unrelated.
1824	> *Market utilization ratio near 100% will DoS deposits as harvest tries to withdraw and reverts*
1825	> *Frozen/paused Market that is harvested from in StakedEXA will DoS deposits leading to loss of yield*
1826	> *Setting a new market will make depositing to the market impossible when harvesting, DoSing deposits*
1827	> *Withdrawals can fail due to deposits reverting in `completeQueuedWithdrawal()`*
1828	> *ETH withdrawals from EigenLayer always fail due to `OperatorDelegator`'s nonReentrant `receive()`*
1829	
1830	**Interrogate the pause switches.** Pausing is meant to be selective and reversible. Check that pausing one thing does not block another that must stay live (repay, liquidate, withdraw), that the pause can actually be applied as documented, and that unpausing restores state.
1831	> *Cannot repay or liquidate on paused asset*
1832	> *Admin will not be able to only pause deposits in the `Vault` due to incorrect check leading to DoSed withdrawals*
1833	> *Withdrawals and Claims are meant to be pausable, but it is not possible in practice*
1834	> *`SpiritFactory` won't be able to stop the Airstream contract*
1835	
1836	**Brick the upgrade or the config.** Permanent loss of administrative control is a real finding when it makes the contract unfixable.
1837	> *Admin will not be able to upgrade the smart contracts, breaking core functionality and rendering the upgradeable contracts useless*
1838	> *FeeManager's admin cannot grant or revoke any role*
1839	> *Incompatibility of Upgradeability Pattern in TitlesGraph Contract*
1840	> *Changing the epoch duration will completely break the vault and the slashers*
1841	
1842	**Trap value with a state machine.** A state that cannot be exited, a request that cannot be cancelled, a flag that cannot be cleared, a threshold that can never be met.
1843	> *`FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPercentage()` uses 540 instead of `540 days` leading to stuck funds*
1844	> *It's impossible to retrieve collected fines from the yield staking contract*
1845	> *Unhandled request invalidation by the owner of Etherfi will lead to stuck debt*
1846	> *Users cannot unstake from YiedlETHStakingEtherfi.sol, because YieldAccount.sol is incompatible with ether.fi's WithdrawRequestNFT.sol*
1847	> *Aura/Convex rewards are stuck after DOS*
1848	
1849	**Overwrite index zero.** Sentinel-value bugs where "not found" returns 0 and the caller writes to slot 0, destroying a real entry.
1850	> *In OstiumTradingStorage, `firstEmptyTradeIndex()` and `firstEmptyOpenLimitIndex()` overwrite index 0 if not found*
1851	
1852	## Escalate before reporting
1853	
1854	A DoS very often conceals a theft: while withdrawals are blocked, does the rate drift? Can the attacker withdraw during the window? Does the blocked liquidation let them keep an underwater position? Push every DoS to its worst variant before writing it up.
1855	
1856	## Every finding needs the cost
1857	
1858	State the attacker's cost (gas, capital, whether the capital is recoverable), the duration of the block (permanent vs bounded — say which), and who cannot do what. A DoS an attacker cannot afford to sustain is a LEAD.
1859	# Shared Lens Rules
1860	
1861	## Bundle contents
1862	
1863	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1864	
1865	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1866	
1867	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1868	
1869	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1870	
1871	## Mandatory reasoning protocol
1872	
1873	Four markers. Each has a trigger. When the trigger fires you MUST emit the marker before continuing. Markers live in your working text — they do NOT go inside FINDING/LEAD blocks.
1874	
1875	| Trigger | Marker | Content |
1876	| --- | --- | --- |
1877	| You open a function that moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Explain in plain English what a user gives, what they get, and which totals change. No Solidity jargon — no `safeTransfer`, `mload`, `shares`, `wad`. Where you have to reach for a Solidity term to stay accurate, mark that spot: that is where the bug is. |
1878	| You stop on a line whose purpose is not immediately obvious | `[Why: <file:line>]` | One question that drills past "because that is how it is written." If your answer restates the code, ask again. Stop when the answer exposes the implicit belief the code rests on. |
1879	| A path reads as clean, or a guard looks sufficient | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Three concrete attacker moves against it. Specific addresses, values, and states — never abstractions. |
1880	| You finish a lifecycle from the money map | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | Walk every user withdrawing in the worst order. State explicitly whether the last one gets paid in full, and if not, by how much the protocol is short. |
1881	
1882	Heavy use of these is what produces the audit. Skipping them yields surface-level scanning, which is the failure mode of every junior auditor. The orchestrator checks marker counts.
1883	
1884	## Saturation is mandatory
1885	
1886	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1887	
1888	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1889	
1890	## Do not report
1891	
1892	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1893	
1894	## Output
1895	
1896	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1897	
1898	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1899	
1900	```
1901	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1902	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1903	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1904	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1905	path:
1906	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1907	  2. state changes to Y
1908	  3. actor does Z
1909	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1910	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1911	```
1912	
1913	```
1914	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1915	smell: what you found
1916	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1917	description: one sentence on the trail
1918	```
1919	
1920	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1921	
1922	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.
1923

1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).
