1652	# The 0xSimao Method
1653	
1654	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1655	
1656	## The core thesis
1657	
1658	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1659	
1660	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1661	
1662	| Drift | Shape |
1663	| --- | --- |
1664	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1665	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1666	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1667	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1668	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1669	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1670	
1671	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1672	
1673	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1674	
1675	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1676	
1677	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1678	
1679	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1680	
1681	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1682	
1683	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1684	
1685	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1686	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1687	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1688	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1689	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1690	
1691	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1692	
1693	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1694	
1695	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1696	
1697	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1698	
1699	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1700	| --- | --- | --- |
1701	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1702	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1703	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1704	
1705	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1706	
1707	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1708	
1709	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1710	
1711	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1712	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1713	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1714	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1715	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1716	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1717	
1718	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1719	
1720	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1721	
1722	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1723	
1724	Canonical sequences to run:
1725	
1726	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1727	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1728	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1729	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1730	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1731	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1732	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1733	
1734	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1735	
1736	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1737	
1738	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1739	
1740	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1741	
1742	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1743	
1744	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1745	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1746	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1747	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1748	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1749	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1750	
1751	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1752	
1753	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1754	
1755	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1756	
1757	After every finding:
1758	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1759	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1760	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1761	
1762	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1763	
1764	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1765	
1766	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1767	
1768	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1769	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1770	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1771	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1772	
1773	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1774	
1775	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1776	
1777	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1778	
1779	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1780	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1781	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1782	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1783	
1784	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1785	
1786	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1787	
1788	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1789	
1790	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1791	
1792	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1793	
1794	## Do not report
1795	
1796	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1797	# Lens 9 — Access, Authorization & Trust Boundaries
1798	
1799	You own the question of **who is allowed to do what, and whether the code actually enforces it.**
1800	
1801	Not "this function is `onlyOwner`, is the owner trusted?" — that is not a finding. What you hunt is: a function that should check something and does not; a check that validates the wrong thing; a privileged role whose legitimate powers compose into theft; and every entry point the team forgot is an entry point.
1802	
1803	## Attack surfaces
1804	
1805	**Enumerate the real entry points.** List every `external`/`public` function and every callback, hook, receiver, and `fallback`. Callbacks are the ones teams forget: flash-loan handlers, cross-chain receivers, ERC721/1155 receivers, AMM swap callbacks, oracle fulfillments, keeper entry points. For each, ask what the caller is and whether that is checked.
1806	> *Funds may be stolen by calling `onMoreFlashLoan()` directly*
1807	> *ConnextHandler `executeFailedWithUpdatedArgs(...)` reentrancy allowedCaller can steal all ConnextHandler tokens*
1808	> *In BaseRouter, the beneficiary isn't checked when starting a flashloan action and it replaces the previous beneficiary*
1809	
1810	**Find the missing owner check.** Functions operating on someone else's position, NFT, or balance that never verify the caller owns it. Look especially at burn, close, cancel, adjust, and claim.
1811	> *`deTokenize()` is missing access control, anyone can burn other people's nfts*
1812	> *Anyone can get the NFT collateral token after an Auction without bidding due to missing check on msg.sender*
1813	> *Anyone can deposit to DarkpoolAssetManager as the owner can be freely chosen without any implication*
1814	> *`BaseTOFT.sol`: `retrieveFromStrategy` can be used to manipulate other user's positions due to absent approval check*
1815	
1816	**Weaponize approvals.** Any contract that pulls tokens with `transferFrom` using caller-supplied `from`, `token`, or `target` parameters lets an attacker drain anyone who has approved it. This is a total-loss pattern and appears constantly in routers, payment helpers, and zaps.
1817	> *Anyone who is approving `BlueprintV5` contract to spend ERC20 can get drained because `Payment::payWithERC20`*
1818	> *A user with a TapiocaOFT allowance >0 could steal all the underlying ERC20 tokens of the owner*
1819	> *Wrong `tokensToCheck` logic in BaseRouter enables attackers to steal funds*
1820	> *Malicious path can be passed to redeem/withdraw() allowing an attacker to drain the strategy*
1821	
1822	**Validate the target, not just the caller.** A permissioned caller passing an attacker-chosen contract address, market, path, strategy, or fee manager is the same exploit with extra steps. Check that every address parameter is whitelisted or derived, never trusted.
1823	> *TOFT in (m)TapiocaOft contracts can be stolen by calling `removeCollateral()` with a malicious `removeParams.market`*
1824	> *Pool Delegates can steal all the pool's funds by setting a malicious Withdrawal Manager*
1825	> *Fixed term loans can be deployed with a wrong fee manager and possibly steal all funds*
1826	> *Changing providers might lead to lost assets in BorrowingVault and YieldVault*
1827	
1828	**Compose privileged powers into theft.** A role doing its job within its documented bounds, but the bounds are not enforced on-chain and the composition is a rug. This IS reportable when you can name the concrete mechanism and the parameter that is unbounded — unlike bare "centralization risk," which is not.
1829	> *Pool Delegates can set a really high origination fee and steal all pool funds*
1830	> *REBALANCER_ROLE can drain funds by rebalancing in a loop in the BorrowingVault*
1831	> *Any duration can be passed by node operator*
1832	> *A malicious operator will control consensus without risking stake (stake-exit lag exploit)*
1833	> *Malicious operator can alone, with any voting power smaller than quorum, forge a proof*
1834	
1835	**Check CEI and reentrancy on every value-moving path.** External call before state update, including token transfers to attacker-controlled contracts, ERC777/ERC721 hooks, and native sends. Also check the inverse: an over-broad `nonReentrant` on `receive()` that breaks legitimate flows.
1836	> *Checks-effects-interactions pattern is not always followed, which can be used to drain all tokens*
1837	> *ETH withdrawals from EigenLayer always fail due to `OperatorDelegator`'s nonReentrant `receive()`*
1838	
1839	**Verify the proof, the root, and the nullifier — all of them.** In any commitment/proof system, check that every function validates the merkle root, that nullifiers cannot be reused or borrowed, and that the code validates the field it claims to validate. Swapping a nullifier check for a note-footer check reads as correct and is not.
1840	> *MerkleRoot is not validated in all StakingAssetManager functions*
1841	> *`UniswapLiquidityAssetManager::_validateCollectFeesArgs()` validates nullifier instead of note footer*
1842	> *Attackers can include other users' nullifiers to make their funds stuck when adding liquidity to curve*
1843	> *Note footers should not be 0 in `curveRemoveLiquidity()` if the corresponding assetOuts are non null*
1844	
1845	**Take the counterfactual address.** Contracts deployed via CREATE2 or a factory can be claimed by whoever deploys first if initialization is not bound to the deployment.
1846	> *Attacker can gain control of counterfactual wallet*
1847	> *Credentials can be manipulated*
1848	
1849	## Every finding needs the caller
1850	
1851	Name who calls it, what they supply, what check is missing at which line, and what they walk away with. "Lacks access control" without a demonstrated impact path is a LEAD.
1852	# Shared Lens Rules
1853	
1854	## Bundle contents
1855	
1856	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1857	
1858	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1859	
1860	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1861	
1862	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1863	
1864	## Mandatory reasoning protocol
1865	
1866	Four markers. Each has a trigger. When the trigger fires you MUST emit the marker before continuing. Markers live in your working text — they do NOT go inside FINDING/LEAD blocks.
1867	
1868	| Trigger | Marker | Content |
1869	| --- | --- | --- |
1870	| You open a function that moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Explain in plain English what a user gives, what they get, and which totals change. No Solidity jargon — no `safeTransfer`, `mload`, `shares`, `wad`. Where you have to reach for a Solidity term to stay accurate, mark that spot: that is where the bug is. |
1871	| You stop on a line whose purpose is not immediately obvious | `[Why: <file:line>]` | One question that drills past "because that is how it is written." If your answer restates the code, ask again. Stop when the answer exposes the implicit belief the code rests on. |
1872	| A path reads as clean, or a guard looks sufficient | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Three concrete attacker moves against it. Specific addresses, values, and states — never abstractions. |
1873	| You finish a lifecycle from the money map | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | Walk every user withdrawing in the worst order. State explicitly whether the last one gets paid in full, and if not, by how much the protocol is short. |
1874	
1875	Heavy use of these is what produces the audit. Skipping them yields surface-level scanning, which is the failure mode of every junior auditor. The orchestrator checks marker counts.
1876	
1877	## Saturation is mandatory
1878	
1879	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1880	
1881	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1882	
1883	## Do not report
1884	
1885	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1886	
1887	## Output
1888	
1889	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1890	
1891	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1892	
1893	```
1894	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1895	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1896	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1897	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1898	path:
1899	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1900	  2. state changes to Y
1901	  3. actor does Z
1902	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1903	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1904	```
1905	
1906	```
1907	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1908	smell: what you found
1909	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1910	description: one sentence on the trail
1911	```
1912	
1913	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1914	
1915	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.

1552	# Money Map — raffle.fun (`Raffle` ERC-1167 clone + `RaffleFactory`)
1553	
1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).

1652	# The 0xSimao Method
1653	
1654	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1655	
1656	## The core thesis
1657	
1658	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1659	
1660	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1661	
1662	| Drift | Shape |
1663	| --- | --- |
1664	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1665	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1666	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1667	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1668	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1669	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1670	
1671	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1672	
1673	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1674	
1675	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1676	
1677	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1678	
1679	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1680	
1681	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1682	
1683	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1684	
1685	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1686	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1687	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1688	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1689	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1690	
1691	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1692	
1693	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1694	
1695	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1696	
1697	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1698	
1699	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1700	| --- | --- | --- |
1701	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1702	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1703	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1704	
1705	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1706	
1707	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1708	
1709	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1710	
1711	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1712	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1713	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1714	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1715	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1716	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1717	
1718	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1719	
1720	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1721	
1722	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1723	
1724	Canonical sequences to run:
1725	
1726	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1727	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1728	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1729	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1730	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1731	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1732	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1733	
1734	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1735	
1736	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1737	
1738	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1739	
1740	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1741	
1742	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1743	
1744	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1745	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1746	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1747	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1748	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1749	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1750	
1751	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1752	
1753	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1754	
1755	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1756	
1757	After every finding:
1758	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1759	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1760	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1761	
1762	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1763	
1764	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1765	
1766	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1767	
1768	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1769	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1770	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1771	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1772	
1773	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1774	
1775	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1776	
1777	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1778	
1779	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1780	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1781	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1782	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1783	
1784	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1785	
1786	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1787	
1788	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1789	
1790	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1791	
1792	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1793	
1794	## Do not report
1795	
1796	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1797	# Lens 10 — Integration & Environment Assumptions
1798	
1799	You own every assumption the code makes about something it does not control: external protocols, token behavior, oracles, and the chain itself.
1800	
1801	The method is always the same. Find the assumption, then find the real-world instance that violates it. A finding here is only real when you can **name the specific token, pool, feed, or chain** that breaks it.
1802	
1803	## Token behavior
1804	
1805	The protocol's own docs usually claim which tokens are supported. Check the code against that claim in both directions — unsupported behavior that is not blocked, and supported behavior that is not handled.
1806	
1807	- **Fee-on-transfer** — received ≠ requested. Any code storing the requested amount is now over-crediting.
1808	  > *Fee on transfer tokens transfer less tokens than what is stored in the receipt on deposits*
1809	  > *`LenderCommitmentGroup` pools will have incorrect exchange rate when fee-on-transfer tokens are used*
1810	- **No revert on failure** (USDT-era, some bridged tokens) — an ignored return value means a silent no-op that still credits the user.
1811	  > *Anyone can steal pool shares from lender group if no-revert-on-failure tokens are used*
1812	- **Non-standard approve** — USDT reverts on non-zero→non-zero; `safeApprove` reverts on the same.
1813	  > *`safeApprove(...)` reverts if approval is different than 0, use `safeIncreaseAllowance(...)` instead*
1814	  > *`PreDepositVault` will not work for USDT*
1815	  > *`FlashRolloverLoan_G5` will not work for certain tokens due to not setting the approval to `0` after repaying a loan*
1816	- **Blacklists** — a blacklisted address in a batch or a forced push-transfer bricks the path.
1817	  > *If wLP is blacklisted, then user will not be able to withdraw it*
1818	- **Rebasing / non-18 decimals / zero-transfer reverts** — check each against what the docs promise.
1819	  > *Rebasing tokens are not supported contrary to the readme and will lead to loss of funds*
1820	  > *Missing several `safeERC20` functions*
1821	
1822	## Oracles
1823	
1824	- Missing or wrong staleness, round-completeness, and min/max-answer checks; and what the fallback returns.
1825	  > *WSTETHPriceFeed returns USD price instead of EUR on oracle failure*
1826	  > *Attacker can trigger temporary shutdown due to RedStonePriceFeedBase missing gas check*
1827	- Timestamps that can be set in the future, causing underflow in a staleness subtraction.
1828	  > *API3 oracle timestamp can be set to future timestamp and block API3 Oracle usage to make code revert in underflow*
1829	  > *API3 oracle future timestamp causes temporary DoS via underflow*
1830	- Rates derived from a vault or LP that can be donated to, and spot reads dressed as price feeds.
1831	  > *SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate*
1832	- Feed availability on every chain the protocol claims to deploy on.
1833	  > *Witnet is not available on some networks listed*
1834	
1835	## External protocol coupling
1836	
1837	Read the integrated protocol's actual interface and semantics — do not assume. Version differences, return-value meanings, and callback requirements are where these break.
1838	
1839	> *Users cannot unstake from YiedlETHStakingEtherfi.sol, because YieldAccount.sol is incompatible with ether.fi's WithdrawRequestNFT.sol*
1840	> *AaveV3 RewardsController provides rewards in any token, should be handled separately*
1841	> *Aave rounding behavior allows malicious users to drain accumulated yield via small withdrawals*
1842	> *`FlashRolloverLoan_G5` will fail for `LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart` due to `CollateralManager` pulling collateral from `FlashRolloverLoan_G5`*
1843	> *Incorrect selector in `FlashRolloverLoan_G5::_acceptCommitment()` does not match `SmartCommitmentForwarder::acceptCommitmentWithRecipient()`*
1844	> *`CurveAssetManagerHelper::_validateAssets()` should check that the number of assets provided is smaller than the maximum of the pool*
1845	> *Curve multi exchange does not validate assetIn and assetOut against route*
1846	> *Stuck ETH in Curve exchanges due to sending `msg.value` to the exchange instead of `amountIn`*
1847	
1848	Check every hardcoded address against the chain it will run on, and every hardcoded selector against the real interface.
1849	> *AaveETHYieldBackend uses wrong WETH address for Polygon (returns WETH instead of WPOL)*
1850	
1851	## Chain environment
1852	
1853	- **zkSync** — `transfer`/`send` gas stipend semantics differ; contract addresses differ from EVM CREATE2; `block.timestamp` behavior and time-sensitive logic need review.
1854	  > *Time-sensitive contracts deployed on zkSync*
1855	  > *Potential ETH Loss Due to transfer Usage in Requestor Contract on `zkSync`*
1856	- **L2 sequencer** — downtime and forced-inclusion delay windows against liquidations and oracle staleness.
1857	  > *Inconsistent sequencer unexpected delay in DelayBuffer may harm users calling `forceInclusion()`*
1858	- **Precompiles and gas** — availability differs per chain; hardcoded gas limits break where opcode pricing differs.
1859	  > *BlsBn254 is not available in certain chains due to hardcoded gas limit*
1860	- **Address identity** — the same address is a different entity on a different chain.
1861	  > *Lost nfts due to smart wallets having different addresses on different chains*
1862	
1863	## Also check
1864	
1865	Upgradeability wiring: missing `__X_init()` calls, storage-gap changes, initializers left unprotected, and pattern mismatches. And re-check that previously-reported issues from earlier audits were actually fixed — he reports regressions as findings.
1866	> *Issue #497 'Add parameter to lender accept bid for MaxMarketFee' from previous audit is still present*
1867	
1868	## Every finding needs the named instance
1869	
1870	"Does not handle fee-on-transfer tokens" is a LEAD. "USDT on mainnet reverts here because approve is called non-zero→non-zero at Line 214" is a finding. Name the token, the feed, the pool, or the chain.
1871	# Shared Lens Rules
1872	
1873	## Bundle contents
1874	
1875	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1876	
1877	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1878	
1879	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1880	
1881	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1882	
1883	## Mandatory reasoning protocol
1884	
1885	Four markers. Each has a trigger. When the trigger fires you MUST emit the marker before continuing. Markers live in your working text — they do NOT go inside FINDING/LEAD blocks.
1886	
1887	| Trigger | Marker | Content |
1888	| --- | --- | --- |
1889	| You open a function that moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Explain in plain English what a user gives, what they get, and which totals change. No Solidity jargon — no `safeTransfer`, `mload`, `shares`, `wad`. Where you have to reach for a Solidity term to stay accurate, mark that spot: that is where the bug is. |
1890	| You stop on a line whose purpose is not immediately obvious | `[Why: <file:line>]` | One question that drills past "because that is how it is written." If your answer restates the code, ask again. Stop when the answer exposes the implicit belief the code rests on. |
1891	| A path reads as clean, or a guard looks sufficient | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Three concrete attacker moves against it. Specific addresses, values, and states — never abstractions. |
1892	| You finish a lifecycle from the money map | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | Walk every user withdrawing in the worst order. State explicitly whether the last one gets paid in full, and if not, by how much the protocol is short. |
1893	
1894	Heavy use of these is what produces the audit. Skipping them yields surface-level scanning, which is the failure mode of every junior auditor. The orchestrator checks marker counts.
1895	
1896	## Saturation is mandatory
1897	
1898	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.
1899	
1900	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.
1901	
1902	## Do not report
1903	
1904	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.
1905	
1906	## Output
1907	
1908	FINDINGs have a concrete, unguarded, exploitable path with a named victim. LEADs have a real accounting or logic smell with a partial path. Default to LEAD over dropping — never drop.
1909	
1910	**One vulnerability per block.** Same root cause = one block. Needs a different fix = separate block.
1911	
1912	```
1913	FINDING | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1914	root_cause: the defect at File.sol:LINE, naming the missing or wrong operation
1915	internal_pre: protocol state required, or None
1916	external_pre: market/oracle/chain conditions required, or None
1917	path:
1918	  1. actor does X with concrete amount
1919	  2. state changes to Y
1920	  3. actor does Z
1921	impact: who loses what, and who is left holding the loss
1922	mitigation: the single smallest change that removes the defect
1923	```
1924	
1925	```
1926	LEAD | contract: Name | function: func | bug_class: kebab-tag | group_key: Contract | function | bug-class
1927	smell: what you found
1928	unverified: precisely what you could not establish
1929	description: one sentence on the trail
1930	```
1931	
1932	`group_key` drives deduplication and is always `ContractName | functionName | bug_class`.
1933	
1934	An `internal_pre` or `external_pre` of `None` is the strongest possible finding — never pad these to look thorough. State the truth.

1553	
1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).

1652	# The 0xSimao Method
1653	
1654	Derived from 869 published findings across 143 reviews. This is HOW to think. Your lens file is WHAT to look for. Work them together.
1655	
1656	## The core thesis
1657	
1658	Most auditors read code looking for bad lines. That finds the bugs a linter finds.
1659	
1660	0xSimao reads code looking for **a claim that has drifted from what actually backs it**. Value moves through a protocol in sequences: deposit, accrue, borrow, liquidate, withdraw. Each step writes some subset of the accounting state, and drift is any way that state stops describing reality:
1661	
1662	| Drift | Shape |
1663	| --- | --- |
1664	| The write is missing | value moved and no variable recorded it — or one branch updates it and the sibling branch does not |
1665	| The write is wrong | the variable is updated with the wrong amount, direction, rounding, units, or decimals |
1666	| The write is mistimed | the right value at the wrong moment, so someone's snapshot is taken against state that is about to change |
1667	| The write goes to the wrong party | the total is intact; the split between cohorts is not |
1668	| The input was never trustworthy | the number is faithfully propagated from an oracle, a live balance, or a caller-supplied parameter an attacker controls |
1669	| The state is unreachable | the accounting is correct but a revert, a pause, an unbounded loop, or a missing path means it can never be settled |
1670	
1671	The drift is invisible at any single line. It only appears when you ask: *after this whole sequence, does the protocol still owe exactly what it holds — and can everyone actually collect it?*
1672	
1673	A defect nobody can be shown to lose money from is a curiosity. So every candidate gets one more question, and it is the one that separates a finding from a smell:
1674	
1675	> **Who is left holding the loss?**
1676	
1677	Answer with a named class of actor, never "users". For accounting drift it is often whoever withdraws last, because a shortfall stays invisible until the balance runs out — but for a bricked liquidation it is the solvent lenders eating the bad debt, for a mistimed snapshot it is the cohort that held through the accrual, and for a forged signature it is whoever the forged message was drawn against. If the only person worse off is the caller, there is no finding.
1678	
1679	**This lens is the sharpest one, not the only one.** Accounting drift is the largest single class in his corpus, but it is not the majority of it. The rest is DoS and permanently stuck funds, access control and signature defects, token- and integration-behaviour assumptions (`USDT` approvals, fee-on-transfer, blacklists, pausable collateral), oracle and parameter validation, and cross-chain state — and those are what your lens file owns. Work the money map first because it is what makes the drift class visible; then work your lens on its own terms. When the target has little accounting to speak of — a router, a registry, a verifier, a signature scheme — say so, keep the money map short, and go straight to your lens. Do not force a finding into the drift frame to make it sound like his.
1680	
1681	## Phase 0 — Learn the protocol's own vocabulary before reading for bugs
1682	
1683	His findings are written in the protocol's language: `cdsPoolValue`, `abond`, `downsideProtected`, `unassignedEarnings`, `raBalance`, `floatingBackupBorrowed`. He does not audit "a vault"; he audits *this* vault's specific accounting model.
1684	
1685	Before hunting, be able to state in plain English:
1686	- What does a user give, and what claim do they receive in return?
1687	- What is that claim worth, and which variables determine the value?
1688	- Where does yield come from, and who is entitled to it?
1689	- What happens when the protocol is short — who absorbs the shortfall?
1690	
1691	If you cannot answer these without Solidity jargon, you are not ready to find his class of bug. Any spot where your plain-English explanation goes fuzzy is exactly where the bug is; mark it and come back.
1692	
1693	## Phase 1 — Build the money map
1694	
1695	For every storage variable that claims to be an aggregate — `total*`, `*Supply`, `*Balance`, `*Deposited`, `*Locked`, `*Reserve`, `*Debt`, `*Accrued`, indices, cumulative rates — enumerate **every** function that writes it and whether that write increases or decreases it.
1696	
1697	Then build the asymmetry table. Three columns of pure gold:
1698	
1699	| Asymmetry | What to look for | Real finding |
1700	| --- | --- | --- |
1701	| Moved without tracking | value transferred out with no matching decrement | *"Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry"* |
1702	| Tracked in one branch only | `if` updates the total, `else` does not | *"Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to `VaultPoolLib::redeem()` not always decreasing `raBalance` and `paBalance`"* |
1703	| Never tracked at all | a balance is real but no variable represents it | *"Total `ETH`, `WETH` and `gameETH` are not tracked which will lead to insolvency"* |
1704	
1705	Also flag every place a **live balance read** (`token.balanceOf(address(this))`, `address(this).balance`) is used as an accounting source. That is a donation attack or a cross-user theft waiting to happen — *"`ManagedLeveragedVault::openDen()` using all `asset()` balance"*, *"SDAIPriceFeed is vulnerable to donation attack via manipulatable vault rate"*.
1706	
1707	## Phase 2 — Write the invariants down
1708	
1709	5–15 statements that must always hold. Concretely, not vaguely:
1710	
1711	- `Σ(all user withdrawable) <= actual token balance` — the solvency invariant, his single most productive one
1712	- `totalX == Σ userX` for every aggregate with a per-user counterpart
1713	- every credited unit is debited exactly once, in exactly one place
1714	- monotonic things (indices, cumulative rates, timestamps) never go backwards and cannot be advanced for free
1715	- a user's claim cannot increase from an action that costs them nothing
1716	- state on chain A and chain B agree after every message settles
1717	
1718	An invariant you can state and then break with a sequence is a finding. An invariant the docs assert and the code does not enforce is his highest-yield source of all.
1719	
1720	## Phase 3 — Run the lifecycles, not the functions
1721	
1722	Do not audit function by function. Audit *sequences*, and after each step write down which accounting variables changed and which should have.
1723	
1724	Canonical sequences to run:
1725	
1726	1. deposit → accrue yield → withdraw
1727	2. deposit → borrow → price moves → liquidate → withdraw
1728	3. stake → rewards distributed → unstake → claim
1729	4. deposit → withdraw → deposit again (re-entry into the same accounting slot — *"Borrower deposit, withdraw, deposit will reinit `omniChainData.cdsPoolValue`"*)
1730	5. open → adjust position → close (does the adjust path keep every invariant the open path established? — *"The health of a `ProtectedListing` is incorrectly calculated if `tokenTaken` has been changed through `adjustPosition()`"*)
1731	6. source chain send → destination chain receive → failure/retry
1732	7. the same sequence at expiry / after maturity / after the vault has ended
1733	
1734	For each, ask at every step: **what did we just change that something else still assumes the old value of?**
1735	
1736	## Phase 4 — Attack across cohorts and across time
1737	
1738	This is the most distinctive part of his method, and the least commonly imitated.
1739	
1740	Value in DeFi is split pro-rata among a changing set of holders. Any calculation that uses a *current* total to distribute a *historically accumulated* amount lets someone join late and take a share of value they did not earn.
1741	
1742	Three questions, applied to every distribution, reward, fee, yield, and profit path:
1743	
1744	1. **Can I join immediately before a distribution and take a share of it?**
1745	   *"Immediately start getting rewards belonging to others after staking"*, *"Late abond holders steal USDa amount from liquidations from earlier abond holders"*, *"increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction"*
1746	2. **Can I leave immediately before a loss and push it onto whoever stays?**
1747	   *"Borrower withdrawing at a loss will cause losses for cds depositors that only withdraw after the price recovers"*
1748	3. **The Last User Out test.** Have every user withdraw, in sequence, in the worst order. Does the last one get paid? If the protocol is short by even dust, the money map has a leak upstream — go find it.
1749	   *"`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent"*
1750	
1751	Cumulative-rate and index-based accounting deserves special hostility: check whether the index can be advanced without cost (*"Malicious user can call `calculateCumulativeRate()` any number of times to inflate debt rate as `lastEventTime` is not updated"*), and whether a user's snapshot is taken at the right moment (*"Depositing to another receiver other than `msg.sender` will lead to stuck funds by increasing `avgStart` without claiming"*).
1752	
1753	## Phase 5 — Saturate the subsystem
1754	
1755	When you find one bug, **do not move on**. His reports cluster: 38 findings in one protocol, most in a single accounting subsystem. That is not luck. Once the accounting model is in your head, mine it out.
1756	
1757	After every finding:
1758	1. Search the codebase for every other site with the same code shape — by function name *and* by pattern. If `redeem()` forgets a decrement, check `withdraw()`, `emergencyWithdraw()`, `redeemExpired()`, and the cross-chain variant.
1759	2. Attack the other branches of the function where you found it.
1760	3. Escalate: a DoS often conceals fund theft; a rounding error often compounds into drain. Push each finding to its worst exploitable variant before writing it up.
1761	
1762	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure, not an omission.
1763	
1764	## Phase 6 — Prove it, with preconditions stated honestly
1765	
1766	His writeups make the reader's job trivial by separating what the protocol must look like from what the world must look like:
1767	
1768	- **Internal pre-conditions** — protocol state required (a maturity exists, a position is near liquidation, deposits are non-zero). "None" is common and is the strongest possible case.
1769	- **External pre-conditions** — market/oracle/chain conditions required (price moves X%, sequencer down, gas above Y). "None" is again the strongest case.
1770	- **Attack path** — numbered, concrete, with actors and numbers. Not "an attacker could manipulate the rate" but "1. User deposits 100e18. 2. User is liquidated via `liquidationType1()`, adding 5e18 USDa. 3. Attacker deposits via flashloan and withdraws, taking 4.9e18 of it."
1771	- **Impact** — who loses what. Name the victim class.
1772	
1773	If you cannot fill the attack path with real numbers, you have a LEAD. Say so. A well-described lead is worth more than a finding you inflated.
1774	
1775	## Phase 7 — Minimal mitigation
1776	
1777	One change, the smallest that removes the defect, stated in the protocol's own terms:
1778	
1779	- "Add a cumulative tracking variable to handle this case."
1780	- "Set the vesting interest to 0 when the new interest is 0."
1781	- "Decrease `raBalance` in the early-redemption branch as well."
1782	- "Use `mulDiv` when converting between token and share amounts."
1783	
1784	Not "refactor the accounting system." Not "consider adding validation." Name the operation to add, remove, or reorder.
1785	
1786	## Three habits that separate his findings from noise
1787	
1788	**Root cause is a missing operation at a named line.** Very often the bug is not a wrong line but an absent one. Write it that way: *"In `PsmLib.sol:125`, `self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount)` is not called."* Pointing at the absence is what makes the fix obvious.
1789	
1790	**Judge what the code allows, never what the deployer intends.** "The admin wouldn't do that" is not a mitigation. But equally, "admin can rug" with no concrete mechanism is not a finding.
1791	
1792	**Doubt the clean-looking path hardest.** The functions that read as obviously correct are the ones everyone else also skipped. When a guard looks sufficient, name three specific ways to defeat it — with addresses, values, and states, not abstractions — before you accept it.
1793	
1794	## Do not report
1795	
1796	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Standard, accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a swap the user chose, rounding dust with no amplification, first-depositor inflation where `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` or a virtual-share offset is already present). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" with no mechanism. Gas optimizations dressed as vulnerabilities. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters.
1797	# Lens 11 — Edge & Terminal States
1798	
1799	You own the states the developers never tested: empty, single, first, last, zero, maximum, expired, paused, ended, and cancelled.
1800	
1801	Code is written for the steady state — many users, non-zero balances, an ongoing period. Almost every function has at least one boundary where its assumptions quietly stop holding, and the terminal states (expiry, vault ended, program finished, last user) are where the accounting bugs concentrate because nobody re-derives the math for them.

1803	## The checklist — run every one against every stateful function
1804	
1805	**Zero / empty.** `totalSupply == 0`, no depositors, no stakers, zero rewards, zero amount, empty array. What does the division do? Where do distributed tokens go when there is nobody to receive them?

1807	> *Having no deposits in `StakedEXA` will lead to stuck rewards when harvesting*
1808	> *Utilization rates are 0 when average assets are 0, which may be used to game maturity borrows / deposits / withdrawals*
1809	> *Unconditional lastUpdated advance in RangePool.sync leads to loss of streamed BMX when pool liquidity == 0*
1810	
1811	**One / sole occupant.** A single participant, one wei, one share, the only LP. Strict `<` guards frequently exclude the legitimate sole-occupant case; verify `<=` is the right comparator on every count check.
1812	> *A malicious user may unlock instantly all the funds from the `FluidLocker` when no one is staking in the Tax pool*
1813	> *`ClearingHouseLiq::_finalizeSubaccount()` does not check if the subaccount has lps*
1814	> *Unassigned pool earnings can be stolen when a maturity borrow is liquidated by depositing at maturity with 1 principal*
1815	
1816	**First.** First depositor, first mint, pool creation, initialization. Who sets the initial rate and can it be set adversarially?
1817	> *`BoldToken` initialization can be frontrun to silently mint/approve bold to an attacker*
1818	> *Incorrect initial deposit calculation may cause cancelProgram to revert*
1819	
1820	**Last.** The last withdrawer, the last share burned, the final unit of supply, the last bond. This is his highest-yield edge: run the full unwind and check whether the final actor is paid and whether residual value is trapped.
1821	> *User to sell the last supply will make the exchange contribution forever stuck*
1822	> *Interest generated by last bond will not go to anyone when liquidating as there is no bond amount to collect it*
1823	> *`totalEarnings` is incorrect when withdrawing after ending which will withdraw too many funds leaving the `Vault` insolvent*
1824	> *Liquidator will leave a pool with unassigned earnings on `Market::clearBadDebt()` free to claim for anyone when the repaid maturity is not the last*
1825	
1826	**Expired / matured / ended.** Every function behaves differently after expiry, and the expiry-path variants are the least reviewed code in any protocol. Re-run the whole lifecycle past the boundary.
1827	> *Users redeeming early will withdraw `Ra` without decreasing the amount locked, which will lead to stolen funds when withdrawing after expiry*
1828	> *Withdrawing all `lv` before expiry will lead to lost funds in the Vault*
1829	> *Expired maturities longer than `FixedLib.INTERVAL` with unaccrued earnings may be arbitraged and/or might lead to significant bad debt creation*
1830	> *`LidoVault::vaultEndedWithdraw` doesn't take into consideration income withdrawals before slashing, blocking variable users from withdrawing their income*
1831	> *`VaultPoolLib::reserve()` will store the `Pa` not attributed to user withdrawals incorrectly and leave it untracked once it expires again*
1832	
1833	**Paused / frozen / halted.** Which functions must remain available while paused (repay, liquidate, withdraw)? Can the pause be applied as documented? What happens to in-flight requests?
1834	> *Cannot repay or liquidate on paused asset*
1835	> *Admin will not be able to only pause deposits in the `Vault` due to incorrect check leading to DoSed withdrawals*
1836	
1837	**Cancelled / reverted / retried.** Cancellation and retry paths must fully undo what the forward path did. They usually undo most of it.
1838	> *Cancelling rounds after finalizing will lead to incorrect `globalTokenAllocPerIDORound` tracking*
1839	> *Method refundPlayers doesn't update `_lockedETH` in WinnableTicketManager*
1840	> *`DrawManager.canStartDraw` does not consider retried RNG requests when determining if a new draw auction can be started*
1841	
1842	**Maximum / saturation / cap.** Full utilization, cap reached, maximum leverage, maximum array length, ratio at exactly 1. Down-casts wrap near saturation, and caps interact badly with pro-rata math.
1843	> *Market utilization ratio near 100% will DoS deposits as harvest tries to withdraw and reverts*
1844	> *Funding cap in `IDOPoolAbstract::_basicParticipationCheck()` is imprecise and can lead to excessive tokens sold*

1846	> *Yield loss due to `StrategyRouterLib::rebalanceStrategies()` not allocating saturated strategy deposits*
1847	
1848	**Threshold boundaries.** Any comparison against a configured threshold: test exactly at, one below, and one above. Value that falls on the wrong side of a threshold often silently changes owner.
1849	> *In `PCLBaseSwapInside::_compoundRewards()`, if the sellPortion is smaller than rewardSwapThreshold, some of the rewards will move to keepPortion*

1851	> *Protocol will need to donate minimum debt for all new ManagedLeveragedVaults*
1852	
1853	**Reconfiguration mid-flight.** A parameter changed while positions are open: epoch duration, market address, reward duration, provider, multiplier ordering.
1854	> *Changing the epoch duration will completely break the vault and the slashers*

1866	# Shared Lens Rules
1867	
1868	## Bundle contents
1869	
1870	Your bundle is five concatenated parts: all in-scope source, the protocol's **money map** (built by the orchestrator), the **method** (how to think), your **lens** (what you own), and these shared rules (output format and protocol).
1871	
1872	Read the whole bundle once at the start. Do not re-read in-scope files for the initial scan. Read or search the repo only for cross-file lookups or out-of-scope context (`interfaces/`, `lib/`, `mocks/`, `test/`).
1873	
1874	**Start from the money map, not the file list.** Pick the tracked totals, lifecycles, and cohorts your lens owns, and attack those. The file list is where you go to confirm, not where you begin.
1875	
1876	When matching function names, check both `functionName` and `_functionName` (Solidity convention), and check library variants (`XLib::function`).
1877	
1878	## Mandatory reasoning protocol
1879	
1880	Four markers. Each has a trigger. When the trigger fires you MUST emit the marker before continuing. Markers live in your working text — they do NOT go inside FINDING/LEAD blocks.
1881	
1882	| Trigger | Marker | Content |
1883	| --- | --- | --- |
1884	| You open a function that moves value or writes a tracked total | `[Model: <name>]` | Explain in plain English what a user gives, what they get, and which totals change. No Solidity jargon — no `safeTransfer`, `mload`, `shares`, `wad`. Where you have to reach for a Solidity term to stay accurate, mark that spot: that is where the bug is. |
1885	| You stop on a line whose purpose is not immediately obvious | `[Why: <file:line>]` | One question that drills past "because that is how it is written." If your answer restates the code, ask again. Stop when the answer exposes the implicit belief the code rests on. |
1886	| A path reads as clean, or a guard looks sufficient | `[Defeat: <function>]` | Three concrete attacker moves against it. Specific addresses, values, and states — never abstractions. |
1887	| You finish a lifecycle from the money map | `[LastOut: <lifecycle>]` | Walk every user withdrawing in the worst order. State explicitly whether the last one gets paid in full, and if not, by how much the protocol is short. |
1888	
1889	Heavy use of these is what produces the audit. Skipping them yields surface-level scanning, which is the failure mode of every junior auditor. The orchestrator checks marker counts.
1890	
1891	## Saturation is mandatory
1892	
1893	When you find a bug, weaponize the pattern across the entire codebase before moving on. Search by function name AND by code shape. If one redemption path forgets a decrement, check every other redemption, withdrawal, emergency, expiry, and cross-chain variant. Then attack the other branches of the function where you found it. Then escalate the finding to its worst exploitable variant — a DoS often hides fund theft.

1895	A repeat instance you missed is an audit failure.

1898	
1899	Admin-only functions doing admin things. Accepted DeFi tradeoffs (ordinary MEV on a user-chosen swap, rounding dust with no amplification path, first-depositor inflation where a virtual-share offset or `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY` already exists). Self-harm-only bugs. "Centralization risk" or "admin can rug" without a concrete mechanism. Missing zero-address checks on admin setters. Gas findings.

1552	# Money Map — raffle.fun (`Raffle` ERC-1167 clone + `RaffleFactory`)
1553	
1554	Scope: `Raffle.sol` (614 lines), `RaffleFactory.sol` (186), `IRaffle.sol` (521), `IRaffleFactory.sol` (150), `RaffleConstants.sol` (43). Spec: repo-root `DESIGN.md` (included at the top of `source.md`).
1555	
1556	**Empty sections, stated up front:** there are NO shares or exchange rates, NO interest/index accrual, NO price oracles, NO liquidations, NO cross-chain messaging, NO owner/admin/pause/upgrade. The accounting is five USDC liability buckets plus one escrowed NFT per clone. Lenses whose home turf is absent (share-rate, liquidation, cross-chain) should map their lens onto the nearest analogue — the VRF request→callback is the only async two-step flow; the reserve threshold is the only outcome switch; the refund path is the only "withdraw" queue — and report nothing rather than force a finding.
1557	
1558	## Plain-English model
1559	- A sponsor (the `msg.sender` of `RaffleFactory::createRaffle`) escrows exactly one ERC-721 prize into a fresh clone. Buyers pay 1 USDC (1_000_000 raw units) per entry; each purchase mints ONE transferable ticket NFT covering a contiguous inclusive entry range `[firstEntry,lastEntry]`.
1560	- After `endTime`, anyone may pay Chainlink VRF (in native ETH) to draw one entry. Reserve met (`totalEntries >= reserveEntries`) → `NftWon`: winner gets the NFT; 95% sponsorRecipient / 5% treasury. Reserve missed → `CashWon`: winner gets 80% of gross, sponsor 15% (remainder), treasury 5%, NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient.
1561	- If nobody requests a draw within 2 days of `endTime`, or the callback misses its 2-day window, anyone flips the raffle to `Refunding`: each ticket burns for 100% of its entries and the NFT goes back to sponsorRecipient. An empty raffle can be closed by the sponsor any time, by anyone after `endTime`.
1562	- Nobody earns yield. The only parties who can absorb a loss are: buyers (expected 20% haircut in `CashWon` vs. a refund), the draw requester (pays the VRF fee, never reimbursed), secondary-market counterparties of tickets, and whoever holds a claim that can never be collected (no sweep, no expiry, no admin).
